name: Aaron Judge
season_outlook: One of four players in history with four 50-homer seasons, and one of three to hit 50-plus homers while winning the batting title (Jimmie Foxx, 1938; Mickey Mantle, 1956), Judge is baseball's preeminent all-around hitter. He has claimed three of the past four AL MVP awards, covering a span during which he hit .311 with an average of 53 home runs, 116 RBI, 118 runs scored and 114 walks per year. Now 33, Judge has also sufficiently answered the injury question that plagued him earlier in his career, as he has appeared in at least 152 games in three of the past four years, while batting .305/.473/.634 with 16 homers across his final 49 regular-season contests following a 10-day IL stint for an elbow issue in July/August. He's an exemplary choice to begin your draft in any fantasy format.

name: Bobby Witt Jr.
season_outlook: There are five-tool talents, and then there's Witt. He was one of just two players to register at least 90th percentile Statcast metrics in terms of expected weighted on-base average (xwOBA), sprint speed and outs above average defensively (Corbin Carroll was the other) -- and Witt was the only one to also register at least a 90th percentile expected batting average. It's a skill set that solidifies his universal first-round fantasy status, and he'll enter 2026 at a prime-age 25. That his Royals moved the fences in at Kauffman Stadium this season can only help Witt's power prospects, as a return to the 30/30 form he displayed in 2023 and 2024 could be coming.

name: Shohei Ohtani
season_outlook: Baseball's greatest historical two-way player could be primed for his best season yet. On offense in 2025, Ohtani exceeded 50 home runs for a second consecutive season and stole 20-plus bases for a third straight year. On the mound, the Dodgers were uber-conservative with his recovery from his September 2023 elbow reconstruction, but Ohtani delivered per-start numbers in line with his pre-injury rates. His pitching usage also ramped up right in time for the playoffs, during which he became the first player in history to hit three home runs while also striking out 10 batters in one game in the Dodgers' NLCS clincher, triggering memories of his 2022, when he scored 411 fantasy points as a hitter and 475 as a pitcher. As the Dodgers surely will, so must you manage his daily utility -- he can be used as a DH or pitcher, but not both --  but Ohtani's potential puts him head and shoulders ahead of the pack.

name: Jose Ramirez
season_outlook: One of baseball's most consistent, well-rounded players, Ramirez is one of only two with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of the past five seasons, averaging 31.6 and 32.0 over that time. He's also one of only four with at least a batting title-qualified 80% contact rate in all of those years. From a fantasy point-scoring perspective, he has finished top 10 among hitters in each of the past six seasons, which is twice as long as the players with the next-longest such streaks (3, by Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto). Ramirez's 33 years of age raise slight concerns that his decline phase could soon gradually begin, but for 2026, at least, his five-tool ability makes him one of the top picks in any fantasy format.

name: Juan Soto
season_outlook: Although his .224/.352/.393, 8-HR stat line through the first 55 games of 2025 gave the guise of a $765 million contract hangover, Soto's first season with the Mets, on the whole, was anything but. Over the next four months and change, he was fantasy baseball's highest-scoring player (411 points), finishing the year with a career-best 43 home runs while delivering his third consecutive season with at least 100 RBI, 125 walks and a .900 OPS. In an unusual twist, Soto also stole 38 bases, more than he had in the previous four years combined, as he went on an unreal run (pardon the pun) over the season's final two months, seemingly in a quest to join the 40/40 club. That is the facet of his game where regression seems likeliest to strike in 2026, but Soto, still a prime-age 27, remains one of the best players to build around in points leagues and a first-round pick in rotisserie formats.

name: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
season_outlook: Fantasy managers have been (im)patiently awaiting the return of Guerrero's 2021 AL MVP runner-up form. When he finally displayed it, it was during a time when few could reap the rewards. We're talking the 2025 playoffs, where he hit .397/.494/.795 with eight homers in 18 games. That's not to substantially knock Guerrero for his regular-season exploits, as the past five seasons have seen him post the fifth-most fantasy-point average (478.6), the second-most total hits (893) and third-most total bases (1,546). He's a model of consistency with a star's ability to shine at any moment, even if those are sometimes seemingly selective. Still a prime-age 27, Guerrero should be one of your first couple of picks, even if he's not necessarily worthy of being the first.

name: Yordan Alvarez
season_outlook: Alvarez's 2025 was an injury nightmare, from the hand injury he suffered in April -- initially diagnosed as a sprain but ultimately discovered to be a small fracture -- to the season-ending ankle sprain he suffered in September, just 19 games into his return from the prior ailment. It unfortunately continued a pattern of health questions for the Astros slugger who, when healthy, has consistently proven himself to be one of the best all-around hitters in the game. From 2021-24, Alvarez ranked third in OPS (.946) and hard-hit rate (53.8%) and seventh in batting average (.294). Bear in mind that during those 19 late-season, healthy games, he posted significantly better numbers in all three of those categories. A healthy spring training would go a long way towards easing prospective fantasy managers' nerves with this extreme risk/reward pick, but he's far too talented to let slip much further than the first 20 or so picks of any draft.

name: Junior Caminero
season_outlook: Given a chance to play daily for the first time, Caminero broke through in a big way in 2025, his 45 home runs tied for the fourth most in history by a player 22 or younger. It wasn't entirely fueled by the team's one-year stint at hitter-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, either, as Caminero hit more homers on the road (23) than at home (22), though the venue indeed benefited him as a hitter, his OPS 211 points higher in his home games. The move back to pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field for 2026 will raise some alarm bells for Caminero's prospective fantasy managers, but he has some of the best bat speed in baseball and enough contact ability to maintain a high level of impact, regardless of venue. He also finished the year on a high note, batting .291/.353/.615 with 17 homers over his final 47 games, 30 of which were played on the road. Caminero is a franchise building block for fantasy purposes.

name: Corbin Carroll
season_outlook: Carroll rebounded from a disappointing sophomore 2024 -- one in part caused by tweaks he made to his swing the preceding winter that threw off his rhythm -- to register a 30/30 season for the first time in his career. He has now exceeded 400 fantasy points in each of his three complete MLB years, testament to his extra-base ability with the bat and selectivity at the plate. Carroll's .282 isolated power was exceeded by only six other qualified hitters, and he set a personal best with both his fly-ball and Statcast Barrel rates. He'll play 2026 at a prime-age 25, but a broken hamate bone in February cast doubt upon his availability for Opening Day and might require some time to recapture his timing thereafter. Carroll is still capable of first-round fantasy production, but keep tabs on his recovery before spending one of the draft's very first picks on him.

name: Kyle Tucker
season_outlook: Tucker's cumulative 2025 numbers don't remotely do justice to his immense raw talent. Breaking it down by halves, he hit .291/.395/.537 with 17 homers and 20 steals through the season's first three months, which is top 10 in fantasy valuation in both points-based and rotisserie scoring. He then cratered to .225/.348/.342 rates with just five homers and five steals over the final three months, placing outside the top 190 players overall. Following the season, Tucker revealed that he had been playing through a hand fracture suffered in early June, an explanation that affords promise of a complete rebound from him following the winter's rest. The Dodgers are clearly banking on that, granting him the second-highest contract average annual value of any player in history, while placing him in the heart of a loaded lineup. Anticipate Tucker bouncing back and consider him a first rounder still.

name: Kyle Schwarber
season_outlook: One of baseball's best power sources, Schwarber joins Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani as the only hitters with at least 180 home runs and 400 each of runs and RBI over the past four seasons, and his 18.3% Statcast Barrel rate in that time is fourth-best among qualifiers. Schwarber's keen eye at the plate, too, is an asset in points leagues, as his 426 total walks and 15.2% walk rate over that same span rank third and fourth. That he has also improved substantially against left-handed pitchers, posting his two best single-year OPS against them in the past two years, only helps cement his case as a foundational fantasy pick, even as a 33-year-old who can be slotted only at DH (UT).

name: Elly De La Cruz
season_outlook: One of the league's best young power/speed threats, De La Cruz was one of only five players with as many as 50 home runs and 75 steals between the date of his MLB debut (June 6, 2023) and the end of last July -- and the only one with as many as 100 steals over that stretch. Unfortunately, he struggled mightily over the season's final two months, batting just .221/.280/.341 with three homers and eight steals (in 10 attempts) over 52 games, likely as a result of his playing through a partially torn quadriceps. The winter's rest should afford De La Cruz time to sufficiently heal, but his funk served as a reminder that his free-swinging nature at the plate deepens his statistical downside, not to mention is significantly more useful in rotisserie than points-based leagues. To that point, he finished 17th on the 2024 Player Rater, but only 50th in fantasy points scored, so keep that disparity in mind as you weigh your investment in a rebound.

name: Ketel Marte
season_outlook: A shining star at one of the game's thinner positions, Marte has hit at least 25 home runs with an .800 OPS in each of the last three seasons. No other second baseman can claim more than one year of either number. Marte has done it with a combination of elite plate discipline, raw power and contact. In 2025, he put forth his best season from the left side of the plate (.288/.377/.519 rates) since 2019, addressing one of the few previously ordinary facets of his game. The only knocks on Marte now are questions about an eventual career downslope, as he'll play 2026 at age 32, and his injury history, as he has missed at least 25 games in four of the past five seasons. They're minor questions, however, and drafting him as a foundational part of your fantasy team should pay big dividends from a tough-to-fill lineup spot.

name: Cal Raleigh
season_outlook: Raleigh's historic year -- he set single-season records for most home runs by a catcher (60) and drove in more runs (125) than any backstop had in 51 years -- is less subject to regression than you might think. He adopted an extremely fly ball-oriented approach at the plate, posting the highest qualified fly-ball rate in 13 years and the majors' fourth-best Barrel rate. Raleigh's raw power is as legitimate as anyone's in the game, even if it comes at the expense of many strikeouts and a low batting average. It makes him the top catcher, though his fantasy worth ultimately comes down to your league settings. In ESPN leagues, he's such a stalwart at a thin position that he's a borderline first-rounder. In deeper two-catcher leagues, Raleigh's 2025 headlines could cause him to be drafted too aggressively, ignoring the fact that 60 homers is a near impossibility to repeat.

name: Ben Rice
season_outlook: Between his having bulked up, made a batting-stance adjustment and adopted a torpedo bat during the prior winter, Rice's breakthrough last season had plenty of rationale. His hard-hit rate spiked by 20%, and he finished sixth among batting title-eligible hitters in expected wOBA. But perhaps most important for fantasy purposes, Rice put in enough time the plate to qualify at catcher, where his offensive contributions carry far more weight than at first base. Rice could again split time between the two positions, but consider that his 26 homers last season ranked fifth among catcher-eligibles for 2026. He's an up-and-comer well worth an early-round pick.

name: Matt Olson
season_outlook: Olson is a model of durability and elite power, even if his borderline MVP-candidate 2023 season now looks like an outlier. He hasn't missed a game since May 1, 2021, and is the only player with at least 29 home runs and .200 isolated power in each of the past seven full MLB seasons (2018-19, '21-25). As a heart-of-the-order hitter for a Braves lineup that feels like it has been stricken with exceedingly awful luck over the past two seasons, Olson seems a strong bet for another near-30 HR/100 RBI campaign, with the possibility of more power upside. He's worth selecting in the early rounds of any draft.

name: Fernando Tatis Jr.
season_outlook: Finally beyond the injury issues that plagued him for much of his first six MLB seasons, Tatis delivered the most well rounded year of his career to date. Though he posted the lowest HR rate of his career (3.6%, resulting in a total of just 25 taters), he vastly improved his contact and his patience at the plate, setting personal bests with his 73.0% contact and 24.1% chase rates. The result was more fantasy points (439) than Tatis scored in 2021 (422), when he hit 42 home runs, and it sets him up for potentially greater things in 2026 as a 27-year-old. He's not without injury risk based upon his track record, but with his skills now making him nearly as strong a pick in points-based as rotisserie leagues, he's a legitimate building block player for fantasy purposes.

name: Cody Bellinger
season_outlook: Bellinger's skill set is a cavalcade of underlying metric-busting magic. Here are his percentile rankings in various Statcast metrics over the past three seasons combined: 21st in bat speed, 25th in hard-hit rate and 39th in Barrel rate. Nevertheless, Bellinger's three-year averages during that same time are a .281 batting average, 24 homes, 91 RBI and 14 steals -- and he has even earned MVP votes in two of those seasons! Having as elite a contact rate as he does certainly helps, as does his extreme fly ball leaning (which makes him a particularly good fit for Yankee Stadium). Bellinger isn't the MVP example he was in 2019, but he's a plenty useful fantasy player all around, and a near-star in points leagues.

name: Ronald Acuna Jr.
season_outlook: The epitome of a risk/reward player in fantasy baseball, Acuna's career has been highlighted by extreme highs, like his historic 42/75 campaign of 2023, and painful (literally) lows, such as the separate ACL surgeries he has had on each knee in 2021 (right) and 2024 (left). It makes him one tough cookie as far as estimating his draft stock, as he has missed more games over the past five seasons (305) than any player with even a prayer of going among the top-25 picks of any mixed-league draft. However, in Acuna's defense, he has made strides in improving his plate discipline, boosting his fantasy points league stock, over the past three seasons. His contact-quality metrics last year were outstanding and he should be more willing to be aggressive on the basepaths this season as he gets further removed from his most recent ACL operation. Predicting historical outcomes is fantasy folly, but in his age-28 season, Acuna might yet roar back with another stat line for the ages.

name: Nico Hoerner
season_outlook: Hoerner is that rare type of player who always seems to surprise fantasy managers with his year-end grades. He's a noted points-league standout, thanks to his elite contact skills -- he's one of just three players with at least an 85% qualified contact rate in all of the last three seasons. He also has a penchant for doubles and frequent appearances in the upper third of the Cubs lineup. However, Hoerner is also a successful rotisserie player, in that hitters capable of a .300 batting average and 30 stolen bases are a rarity nowadays -- there have only been six such seasons over the past four years, whereas there were six of them alone as recently as 2006. He should be regarded as a near-foundational piece in points leagues, in part due to how thin second base is. Just understand that if you take him early in a rotisserie league, you'll need to make up for his power shortcomings elsewhere on your roster.

name: Julio Rodriguez
season_outlook: After a year away from the 30/30 club, �J-Rod� roared back to that status in 2025, with a campaign that showed relevant growth for points league managers. Rodriguez set a personal best with his 71.8% contact rate, which spiked to 77.4% over the final two months, during which time he hit .299. Between that and the gradual lowering of his ground ball rate from August forward, he could be primed for even bigger things -- perhaps a five-category monster year, or at least a boost in home runs -- as he enters his age-25 season. Rodriguez is a clear first-round talent in rotisserie leagues, but he's also a building-block player in points leagues.

name: William Contreras
season_outlook: Contreras' fantasy production took a downturn in 2025, but it wasn't without explanation, as it was revealed in May that he was playing through a finger fracture dating back to the prior season -- one he endured for the near-entirety of last year. Despite that, his bat warmed along with the summer months, as a .286/.359/.465, 11-HR performance across his final 69 games offers hope that a rebound might be coming, especially after a winter of rest. Now 28, Contreras offers levels of patience and pop that few catchers can, and his 379 combined plate appearances (19% of his total) at DH over the past three seasons give him a rare volume advantage at the position. Continue to regard him one of the premier backstops.

name: Drake Baldwin
season_outlook: Sean Murphy's cracked rib in March paved the way for Baldwin to step in as the Braves' Opening Day catcher, and despite Murphy's lingering presence all year, the lefty slugger made enough of his opportunity that he ultimately captured NL Rookie of the Year honors. Baldwin's is a rare combination of contact, contact quality and raw power. He joined fellow catcher Alejandro Kirk as baseball's only players with at least 400 plate appearances, 10% Statcast Barrel, 45% hard-hit and 80% contact rates. Baldwin also excelled against same-handed pitchers, his almost complete skill set diminishing the chances of a sophomore slump. Although Murphy remains in Atlanta, Baldwin should handle the bulk of the catching duties -- perhaps in a straight platoon, but that's still plenty to make him one of the position's top picks.

name: Brice Turang
season_outlook: A 4-for-35 showing in the postseason couldn't spoil what was an overall offensive breakout for the Brewers' second baseman. Turang went from ranking third in MLB with 50 steals in 2024 to 28th with just 24 steals last season, but he added surprising power and piled up the runs and RBI for a Milwaukee team that ranked third in scoring, with fantasy managers happily accepting the tradeoff for more well-rounded production. Overall, Turang added more than 30 points in batting average and nearly 130 points in OPS to finish neck and neck with Jazz Chisholm at second base in rotisserie leagues. He hits left-handed pitching well enough and seems to have established a new performance baseline, though the batted-ball profile portends a BA closer to .260 than .280 in 2026 and beyond.

name: Shea Langeliers
season_outlook: Last season was a career year for Langeliers, and there were two specific things which held him back from getting even more attention: an oblique injury which cost him some time in the summer, and Cal Raleigh stealing all the spotlight. Langeliers was on a 40-homer pace, and while many will credit the comforts of Sutter Health Park in Sacramento, that would be a mistake as Langeliers hit 19 of his 31 home runs on the road. He increased his power output while also cutting down his strikeout rate from the previous season. The club went as far as to use Brent Rooker in the field despite his defensive limitations to allow Langeliers some half-days off at DH. Langeliers' draft stock has improved as much as any player in baseball, and with all arrows pointing in the right direction, he should be one of the top fantasy catchers in MLB in 2026.

name: Mike Trout
season_outlook: Whether due to injuries or the aging process, Trout is no longer the perennial MVP candidate he once was. Though he played 130 games in 2025 -- more than he had in the previous two seasons combined or in any single year since 2019 -- he hit just .232 with his lowest OPS in any full year (.797). Trout no longer catches up with breaking stuff at his prior Hall of Fame levels, leading to high strikeout totals and lower batting averages, though his power remains excellent (.207 ISO and 93rd-percentile Statcast Barrel rate). The result is a player now similarly valued in roto and points leagues, one now best left to filling out your lineup rather than leading it.

name: Gunnar Henderson
season_outlook: Fresh off a breakthrough 2024 that saw him finish fourth in AL MVP voting, Henderson suffered an intercostal strain five games into spring training that seemed to derail him for most of last year. While he returned to action eight days into the regular season, he never seemed to recapture his prior power stroke, posting a .748 OPS and seven home runs in his first 50 games and reflecting a 5% decrease in his fly-ball rate for the full year. Henderson did, however, maintain his former line-drive stroke as well as his elite speed, swiping a pro-best 30 bases. Perhaps the winter's rest will help him recapture his prior pop. He's a name to track during spring training, as he'll enter 2026 at 24 years old, with MVP-caliber upside if he has a strong showing.

name: Pete Alonso
season_outlook: After setting the Mets' franchise record for home runs in what was the most well-rounded season of his seven-year MLB career, Alonso exercised his opt-out clause to take his wares to Baltimore. There, he'll get to play in a Camden Yards that played much more HR-friendly last season after the team moved the left field fence back in, which presents a good match for a player who just set personal bests in Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates and average exit velocity. Now 31, Alonso has yet to show any signs of the aging curve taking hold, meaning he remains a top fantasy first baseman well worth a selection in the early-to-mid rounds.

name: Bryce Harper
season_outlook: When a 131 wRC+ is your lowest mark since 2019, the bar is clearly high. It is fair to attribute Harper's dip to first-half elbow and wrist issues, the latter requiring a three-plus-week IL stint. However, a look under the hood reveals a low BABIP on outfield line drives that masked Harper's otherwise strong performance. His barrel, hard-hit and strikeout rates were consistent with prior seasons, but unfavorable batted-ball outcomes drove the drop in production. The good news is that a low outfield line-drive BABIP is not a sign of skills deterioration, just poor luck. Still, Harper missed 30 games, continuing a five-year pattern of IL visits. He remains a five-category contributor when healthy, as shown by 12 stolen bases in 14 attempts last season, though durability remains a concern. Harper is no longer a fantasy building block, but his draft stock remains high, as fear of missing out is a strong bias.

name: James Wood
season_outlook: Wood got off to a torrid start to his first full MLB season, batting .278/.381/.534 with 24 homers in 95 first-half games to earn himself an All-Star appearance. The holes in his ground ball-oriented swing, however, caught up with him thereafter, and he hit just .223/.301/.388 with an MLB-leading 105 strikeouts the rest of the way. Wood will need to address those shortcomings, or add some loft to his swing, in order to develop into a true offensive superstar, but few players have the kind of top-shelf metrics in terms of bat speed and contact quality. He's a player to watch during March to see what kinds of adjustments he makes, though as is he's a high-ceiling, early-to-mid-round selection with more upside in rotisserie than points leagues.

name: Manny Machado
season_outlook: Machado authored his seventh All-Star campaign in 2025, winning the Silver Slugger with 27 homers and 95 RBI across 159 games with the Padres during the regular season. The third baseman has fallen just shy of 30 homers the last two years, and his OPS has been under .800 three years running, showing a decreased but still highly respectable performance baseline. At 33 years old, Machado is not much of a runner -- he's grounded into a whopping 41 double plays over the past two seasons -- though he can still chip in a fair number of stolen bases thanks mostly to his veteran instincts. There is still a lot to like here, including durability at a position that sees a sudden drop-off in quality deeper in the player pool.

name: Ozzie Albies
season_outlook: Albies had a season to forget in 2025 with a career-low .671 OPS across 157 games with Atlanta. Adding injury to insult, Albies suffered a hamate bone fracture in his left hand during the final week. He is expected to be fully recovered in time for spring training, but the second baseman's inconsistency in recent years makes him tough to trust entering 2026. Historically, Albies has done a disproportionate amount of his damage from the right side of the plate -- his struggles from the left side have led to calls for him to give up switch hitting. An All-Star as recently as 2023, Albies has shown little in recent years to justify enduring optimism, though at least the downward trends have not yet extended to his overall strikeout rate. Further, the 29-year-old still provides efficiency on the basepaths.

name: Mookie Betts
season_outlook: The aging curve has clearly affected Betts, as his 2025 season saw him post personal worsts in almost every statistical category, not the least of which were his .732 OPS, 35.8% hard-hit rate and 4.3% attempted steals rate. In his defense, however, he dealt with a stomach illness at the season's onset -- something that caused him to lose close to 20 pounds and affected his mechanics at the plate. Betts is fortunately in one of the absolute best environments for propping up counting numbers, as he's surrounded by a cavalcade of lineup all-stars, and he's a contact hitter whose floor isn't as perilous as most. Set your expectations at his three-year averages of a .284 batting average, 26 home runs, 88 RBI and 13 steals and you should be happy with him for the asking price.

name: Nick Kurtz
season_outlook: Kurtz ascended to the majors just one month into the 2025 season, ready to deliver one of the most impressive power displays we've ever seen from a rookie. His 36 home runs were 10th-most in history by a rookie, his 173 OPS+ was second-best in the modern era (minimum 450 plate appearances) and his .329 isolated power was second to only Aaron Judge's .343 in 2017. In fact, Kurtz and Judge are the only players in the 11 Statcast seasons to register at least 15% Barrel and 50% hard-hit rates as rookies (again, 450-PA minimum). That Kurtz only improved as the season progressed eases the worry of any sophomore slump, and he'll still call HR-friendly Sutter Health Park his home in 2026. While history cautions against players repeating the kind of debut that Kurtz just had, he's one of the rare young sluggers with a chance to do it, making him a strong early-round selection.

name: Francisco Lindor
season_outlook: People might call him Mr. Smile, but around these parts, we like to call him Mr. Consistency. Lindor has averaged 32 home runs and 30 stolen bases for the past three seasons and, had he stolen one more base in 2024, he'd have joined Barry Bonds (1995-97) as the only players to go 30/30 in three straight years. Lindor's underlying metrics took a slight step backwards last season, hardly shocking from a then-31-year-old, but that's countered by his being one of the game's most durable players, averaging 158 games the past four seasons. If there's any knock on him, it's that he has a history of somewhat slow starts, his first-half career OPS being 57 points lower than in the second half. Lindor is also questionable for Opening Day following hamate bone surgery in February, which could also extend his tendency for sluggish Aprils. No matter, as if his top-20 overall draft stock isn't to your liking (but it should be!), simply jot down his drafting manager's cell phone number and remember to make a trade-inquiry call around May 15.

name: Freddie Freeman
season_outlook: Freeman is aging like a fine California wine even if he is no longer playing every single game in a season. His days of 100-plus runs and 100-plus RBI appear to be over as his power is waning in his mid-30s, but he is still one of the few five-category producers at his position. He was able to hit .295 last year despite his strikeout rate surging to its highest level since his 2016 season after a long trend of Freeman having one of the better rates in the league. Ideally, Freeman would get some half days at DH, but that is not an option on the Dodgers. Instead, he gets to enjoy hitting behind Shohei Ohtani and Mookie Betts and in front of Will Smith, Max Muncy and Tesocar Hernandez. His 2024-2025 production is very repeatable with his skills and lineup spot, but don't get greedy.

name: Andy Pages
season_outlook: By a show of hands, who had Pages finishing with the second-most home runs on the Dodgers, trailing only Shohei Ohtani? Exactly. Pages provided stability for a roster dealing with injuries throughout the season, appearing in 156 games, mostly in center field, while showing off one of the strongest outfield arms in the league. Pages' chase rate is elevated, but he struck out at a near-league-average rate last season, suggesting improved swing decisions could allow him to rely less on pulled flyballs and more on hitting the ball with greater authority. Stolen-base efficiency remains a concern, as Pages was caught seven times in 21 attempts, and continued issues could earn him the red light.

name: Jackson Chourio
season_outlook: Chourio's first two MLB seasons were almost spot-on as far as counting numbers are concerned. Often, fantasy managers might therefore assume the player has locked in that level of performance expectation, but in his case, remember that Chourio will begin 2026 only 21 years, 15 days old, and he showed glimpses of growth in 2025. His postseason -- .341/.362/.682 rates and four home runs in 12 games, despite dealing with hamstring issues -- was as compelling evidence as any, but he also reflected noticeable jumps in his bat speed and Barrel rate. Besides, he seemed to be turning the corner in early July before the hamstring problem first began. Chourio still has a path to superstardom and, while he's a potentially more profitable pick in rotisserie than points leagues, he's a player you shouldn't let last more than a few rounds in any draft.

name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
season_outlook: Through four months of 2025, Crow-Armstrong seemed on track for top-level MVP votes, in rotisserie terms providing more earnings than any player other than Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani. Regression and his own free-swinging nature at the plate hit Crow-Armstrong hard over the final two months, however, as he hit just .188/.237/.295 and struck out in more than 25% of his trips to the plate. In his defense, Crow-Armstrong's elite speed gives him a steady valuation base in rotisserie leagues, and his Platinum Glove-caliber defense assures him of regular playing time -- which helps boost his points-league value. Improved patience would be his ticket to stardom in the latter, but in the former, he's already a building-block draft pick.

name: Sal Stewart
season_outlook: Stewart is an MLB-ready hitter with growing power who merely needs a defensive place to play. He hit five homers across an 18-game "cup of coffee" with the Reds, playing more at first base than at third, but he'll probably be in the spring mix at both spots due to the team's injury question marks at those positions, although Eugenio Suarez's addition hurt his chances for everyday at-bats. Stewart hit .309/.383/.524 with 20 homers and 17 steals in 118 games between Double-A Chattanooga and Triple-A Louisville last season, and he'll have the Reds' homer-friendly ballpark helping his cause. He's a late-round flier in redrafts as is, and a solid dynasty building block as well.

name: Jose Altuve
season_outlook: Altuve posted a 113 wRC+, his lowest mark in a full season since 2013. While his home-run output climbed to its highest level since 2022, his batting average dipped to a career low outside of the abbreviated 2020 season. A decade ago, that might have been written off as variance, but entering his age-36 season, it may instead point toward the early stages of decline. If that is the case, erosion can accelerate quickly, introducing more risk into a profile that has been remarkably stable for years. Altuve compensated for a modest drop in barrel rate by pulling more flyballs, though there is no guarantee that adjustment sticks. With age, the downside scenarios begin to outweigh the upside, but that reality is typically reflected in the draft cost, and his dual eligibility at second base and outfield still provides some appeal.

name: Alex Bregman
season_outlook: A quadriceps injury he suffered in May derailed what was, at the time, a borderline MVP-caliber start to Bregman's Red Sox career. On May 14, for example, he was sixth among hitters in fantasy points, with significantly better contact-quality metrics than he had displayed in any prior year. Bregman never really recovered at the plate following his mid-July return, though his 154-game average over the three previous seasons (2022-24) suggests his finish was more aberration than the norm. The Cubs seemed to agree by granting him a five-year, $175 million guarantee, where they'll slot him high in what's a solid lineup. It's a good fit for Bregman, who is a great, building-block type of pick in points leagues thanks to his plate discipline and penchant for extra-base hits.

name: Munetaka Murakami
season_outlook: Murakami, who hit 223 home runs over a six-year span (2019-24) in Japan, put off a move to the States one winter ago, only to suffer an injury-plagued 2025 campaign. Between elbow surgery and a nagging oblique issue, he played only 69 games, though his power potential upon his return was as excellent as ever. He hit 24 homers, slugged .659 and had .373 isolated power for the season. The White Sox took a $34 million chance on him to play first base, which at least offers additional positional flexibility for his fantasy managers. Just 26 years old, Murakami is a �three true outcomes� style lefty slugger, which could elicit within White Sox fans memories of Adam Dunn (the Chicago version) on the high end, or Daniel Palka on the low end. Fantasy managers would be best to split the difference and draft accordingly.

name: Oneil Cruz
season_outlook: A hot start to Cruz's 2025 -- he had eight homers and 14 stolen bases through his first 30 games -- seemed to signal the arrival of his long-anticipated breakthrough. However, over time, his former weaknesses continued to squeak through. He posted the third-worst contact rate (66.0%) and 16th-lowest launch angle (8.1 degrees) among batting title-eligibles, capping his power upside. He also hit an abysmal .102/.224/.176 against lefties, rendering him more of a matchups type. Now 27, Cruz still has time to patch those flaws in his game, but he's shaping up as more of a rotisserie-minded breakthrough candidate than a complete, all-around star. Think carefully before reaching for him in points-league drafts.

name: Alec Burleson
season_outlook: Burleson cut his chase rate down and saw immediate results in 2025, slashing .290/.343/.459 across 139 games with the Cardinals to win the Silver Slugger at the utility spot. He improved against lefties and led the team in OPS on the strength of improved patience and selectivity, though he ended up falling short of his 2024 totals in home runs, runs, RBI and steals due to missing time in the second half with a wrist injury. With Willson Contreras now in Boston, Burleson will take over as the everyday first baseman in St. Louis after splitting time between the outfield (74 games), first base (50 games) and DH (22 games) last season. The profile does not look out of place in the middle of a major-league lineup, and entering his age-27 campaign, Burleson still appears capable of more.

name: Will Smith
season_outlook: A Will Smith won another World Series, but Smith is more than just a funny trivia question. He has been a force at the catching position for fantasy managers these past few seasons, even as he lost some of the volume this past year as the designated hitter spot on the roster was re-occupied by Shohei Ohtani. Smith was on pace to best his 2024 production despite the reduction in plate appearances and also went on to post a career-best batting average in 2025. If anything, one could argue the reduced volume was a good thing for Smith to keep him fresh over the course of a full season under the physical demands of catching. This season should be more of the same for playing time and production with a step back toward his career level for batting average with batted-ball luck coming back to previous norms.

name: Randy Arozarena
season_outlook: The only player in history with at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in each of his first five full MLB seasons, Arozarena joins Jose Ramirez as the only players at any point of their career to do that in each of the past five years. That provides Arozarena a strong, top-50 overall base for rotisserie fantasy play, even with his speed metrics declining slightly and this being his age-31 season. He'd need to continue improving his selectivity at the plate, however, to warrant consideration that soon in points leagues, where he's more of a mid-round selection in ESPN formats.

name: Jackson Merrill
season_outlook: Blame injuries, rather than the much-theorized �sophomore slump,� for what ailed Merrill in 2025. A hamstring strain in April, a concussion in June and an ankle sprain in August cost him a combined 44 games and three IL stints, between which he struggled to garner any sort of momentum. It ultimately caused him to attempt zero stolen bases after June 14. Despite this, Merrill sported similarly strong contact-quality metrics to those of his rookie 2024, and he finished the year with a flourish, batting .275/.320/.626 with seven homers and 16 RBI over his final 24 games. Here's hoping that it was a one-year aberration rather than the start of an injury-prone reputation, but Merrill has a lot of rebound potential among players you'll find in the early-to-middle stages of your draft.

name: Byron Buxton
season_outlook: For the first time since 2017, Buxton played more than two-thirds of his team's games last season, though he still made two more trips to the IL (totaling 29 days). OK, we'll still call it a win! Better health led to a complete restoration of his top-shelf raw power and speed metrics and, thanks in part to a career high in plate appearances, he managed another personal best with 35 home runs and was a perfect 24-for-24 stealing bases. Consider it a reminder of what Buxton can contribute at his best, as he's still a close-to-prime 32 years of age albeit with sterling speed metrics. His extensive injury history will -- and should --always keep your draft-day expectations in check. He's also still preferable in rotisserie than in points leagues, but his upside when healthy warrants mid-round consideration.

name: Trea Turner
season_outlook: Turner had back-to-back healthy seasons in 2022 and 2023, but he has hit the injured list both of the two past years, with a hamstring injury at fault in 2025. Turner was still eighth overall in stolen bases despite the hamstring injury, and he remains one of the fastest players in baseball. On some teams, Turner would run every time he reached base, but he also hits in front of Kyle Schwarber and the Phillies do not frequently wish to open up first base and instead rely upon the threat of the steal to help Schwarber see more fastballs. Turner would have scored 100-plus runs had he avoided the injury and is likely thrilled Schwarber is returning to the club. The injury risk is the only thing holding Turner back from being a first-round pick.

name: Maikel Garcia
season_outlook: After finishing third in the majors in stolen bases in 2024, effectively a two-category player (steals and runs), Garcia went all Willie Mays Hayes-in-�Major League 2� last season, inexplicably trading his speed in the quest for power. He attempted only one stolen base across his final 44 games and just five over his final 79, while more than doubling his home run total for the full season. That's not to knock Garcia's improvements as he made huge strides with his selectivity and contact and saw a decent bump in terms of contact quality. We'd, of course, prefer to see him capitalize upon his career best .351 OBP with bushels of steals, which would make him more of an early-round target in rotisserie leagues. As is, he's a solid mid-round pick as he enters his age-26 season.

name: Kevin McGonigle
season_outlook: McGonigle hit .305/.408/.583 in 88 games across three minor-league levels last season, walking 13 more times than he struck out, while hitting 19 homers and stealing 10 bases. He's perhaps the most well-rounded prospect among those with a likely 2026 ETA, and the Tigers have the option of breaking him in at either second base or shortstop once he's ready. McGonigle's skill set is great for all fantasy play, but he's looking like a prospective points-league gem. Consider him a dynasty building block and a �must get� in redrafts the moment he's promoted.

name: Yandy Diaz
season_outlook: Diaz took advantage of his home digs in 2025, hitting 18 of his career-high 25 homers at Steinbrenner Field. He was no slouch on the road with a .780 OPS, but the Rays' move back to Tropicana Field in 2026 looms large as Diaz has 37 homers in 338 career games at the Trop. While he may not have standout power, he has tapped into more in recent years, enough to supplement his high batting average and make Diaz a fantasy standout if not quite a superstar. Primarily a DH at this stage, Diaz retains first-base eligibility for at least one more season, and a case can be made that he's underrated among the wider drafting public. Expect him to continue batting in the top third of the order every single day in his age-34 season.

name: Riley Greene
season_outlook: Greene took his career to another level in 2025, setting career highs in all run production categories, but with a strikeout rate of 30.7 percent. The young outfielder was an everyday player for Detroit because he was so good despite the fact his output against lefties remains a problem. Ten of Greene's 60 homers over the past two seasons have come off lefties, while he has been limited to a .216 average against southpaws. Meanwhile, along with the 50 homers against righties, Greene has a .278/.349./532 slash line versus them. His below-league-average strikeout rate from 2024 rose last season, which ultimately holds back how hopeful anyone can realistically be about BA improvement. The strikeout rate is the same against both righties and lefties. He's a four-category producer at risk of dropping to three if he can't curb the growing swing-and-miss in his stroke.

name: Seiya Suzuki
season_outlook: The Cubs entered the season with an organizational focus on pulling more flyballs, and Suzuki set the tone by increasing his pull rate while maintaining an above-average flyball rate. The approach yielded new career highs with the Cubs in ISO and home runs. That power jump came with a 38-point drop in batting average, though his xBA was only three points lower than the prior season. His strikeout rate ticked down slightly but remained well above league average. Most notably, Suzuki appeared in 151 games, marking his first season since coming over in which he avoided the IL entirely. Often, a year after a major adjustment is used to recalibrate, but Suzuki would be best served sticking with the same approach and hoping his batting average moves closer to his expected mark.

name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
season_outlook: Chisholm and Yankee Stadium represented the perfect marriage, as his first full season in pinstripes saw him pull a career-high 53.3% of batted balls and hit 33.2% in the air (his second-highest single year rate), resulting in his first 30/30 campaign. It did, however, cost him in batting average, as his .242 was his full-season worst, putting more emphasis on his need to steal bases to make up the difference for fantasy. Chisholm's declining speed metrics, and the groin issue that made him more conservative on the basepaths around midseason, raise slight concerns, but he's still one of the better early-round picks you'll find for rotisserie formats. Improving patience over the past two seasons also helps his points-league value, where he's worth a look, albeit one or two rounds later.

name: Adley Rutschman
season_outlook: Just about everything that could possibly have gone wrong for Rutschman in 2025, his age-27 season, did. He hit just .203/.300/.332 across the first two months, made trips to the IL for both obliques (left in June, right in August) and was ultimately pressed for his job by top prospect Samuel Basallo. That competition is the biggest lingering issue, as both players appear likely to make the team in a catcher/DH combination for a team that has a lot of other DH alternatives. Rutschman was previously a budding points-league star thanks to his well-rounded offensive game and the promise of hefty DH time. With that no longer a guarantee, he needs a standout spring to rekindle a top-5 positional valuation in the format. That ceiling remains possible, considering his age and skill set, however.

name: Ian Happ
season_outlook: Happ is entering the final year of his most recent contract, which is something to keep in mind for those who like factors such as contract years when targeting players. Happ has been a consistent on-base machine in recent seasons, but his batting average is now league average as the rest of the league has come down to his level. The switch hitter is at his best when facing righties as most of his homers come from the left side, but he has held his own hitting from the right side of the plate as well in recent years. His on-base abilities lock him in somewhere near the top of the Chicago lineup for 2026, but it will be a different batting order without the presence of Kyle Tucker, and the club's apparent reticence to spend big to replace him. Happ has been a 20/80/80/.240 producer for three straight years and expect a fourth.

name: Corey Seager
season_outlook: Known as a great player with a spotty health history, Seager fell short of 125 games played for the third consecutive regular season, landing at just 102 games with the Rangers in 2025. The shortstop made multiple trips to the injured list early with a hamstring strain and missed the final month following an appendectomy. Even so, he reached 20 homers for the fourth consecutive campaign and for the sixth time in his career, having smacked 30-plus each of the three seasons prior to last. Seager has lost a bit off his batting average in recent years, as his numbers against lefties are in decline, but he still crushes right-handed pitching when available. Steals are not part of the equation and players don't typically get healthier in their 30s, but the five-time All-Star still offers a high upside if he can somehow stay on the field.

name: Taylor Ward
season_outlook: Traded from Anaheim in November, Ward will be part of the new-look Orioles under new skipper Craig Albernaz in 2026. Ward's tenure with the Angels culminated in career highs in home runs (36) and RBI (103) last season, with the outfielder ranking in the top six in the AL in both categories, after previously topping out at 25 homers and 75 RBI in 2024. The right-handed slugger continues to mash lefties, and he at least hits for power against same-side arms if not for batting average. Ward added to his walk rate last season and his offensive contributions more than made up for his defensive limitations. Now 32, Ward should be in position to knock in the runners Pete Alonso leaves on base while batting in the middle of the everyday lineup in Baltimore.

name: Geraldo Perdomo
season_outlook: One of 2025's most unexpected breakthrough performers, Perdomo joined Shohei Ohtani and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only players with at least a .275 batting average, 20 home runs, 20 stolen bases and a 7.0 WAR. Everything clicked for Perdomo, from the counting numbers-inflating 129 starts he made out of the top three spots in the lineup, to the 8.4% HR/FB rate that was more than double his MLB career number entering the year, though those are two areas now subject to some regression. His contact-skills growth represented the bigger story, elevating his floor and making him an ideal points-league pick. So long as you're not expecting a repeat of his 20 homers or 100 RBI, he should be a fine early-to-mid-round pick.

name: Austin Riley
season_outlook: After missing only eight games from 2021 to 2023, Riley played just 110 in 2024 and 102 last season, dealing with a fluke broken hand two years ago and three IL visits for core issues last year. His sports hernia surgery in August should help him re-establish his reliability. Even through the injuries, Riley maintained near-elite exit velocity, barrel rate and hard-hit numbers. However, after slightly improving his strikeout rate from 2021-23, he gave back those gains last year, posting his worst rate since his rookie season. It was likely more a matter of his timing being affected by the injury-driven absences than a change in approach. The market is not quite as bullish as in prior years, but at a thin position full of uncertainty, Riley stands out as a risk worth taking.

name: Christian Yelich
season_outlook: Yelich's 644 plate appearances last season marked his highest total since 2022, while his 29 home runs were his most since 2019. He wasn't quite able to reach 20 steals for a third straight season but was still productive on the basepaths with 16 thefts. He topped 100 RBI for just the second time in his career and finished with a .264/.343/.452 slash line in 150 games. Yelich saw more action than ever at designated hitter with just 19 appearances in the outfield -- which could limit his positional eligibility in 2026 -- and that's unlikely to change much going forward given the back issues he's dealt with throughout his time in Milwaukee. Now entering his age-34 season, Yelich's swing should continue to age well, but some modest regression wouldn't be surprising at this point in his career.

name: Jarren Duran
season_outlook: Duran saw a decline in most areas in 2025 after his first All-Star season the year prior, losing nearly 30 points in batting average along with five homers and 10 steals from his 2024 totals. The outfielder still compiled valuable numbers with 16 HR and 24 SB across 157 regular-season games with the Red Sox while once again leading the American League in triples with 13. He also reached 40 doubles for the second consecutive year, with only Bobby Witt having more two-baggers over the last two seasons. Duran can fly, and his ability to take the extra base boosts his slugging percentage. The right-field dimensions at Fenway Park help the lefty hitter as well, though there have been rumors that Duran could eventually be traded. Even with the drop in performance and lingering uncertainty surrounding his future in Boston, Duran will remain a coveted piece in fantasy.

name: Brandon Nimmo
season_outlook: Nimmo put together another productive campaign in 2025, slugging 25 homers with 92 RBI, both career highs, to go along with 81 runs and 13 steals across 155 games with the Mets. Last season marked his fourth straight reaching 150 games, as Nimmo continues to distance himself from the injury issues that plagued him earlier in his career. In November, he was traded to the Rangers amidst rumors of a rift with former teammate Francisco Lindor, a move that looks like a wash for Nimmo in many respects. The outfielder gave up a bit in terms of OBP and was more aggressive in recent years as he took on more of a run-producer role, but he has the plate skills to transition back to leadoff duty if Texas prefers to go that route.

name: Michael Harris II
season_outlook: Early in 2025, it again looked as though Harris's production would fall short of his skills and athleticism. He went into the All-Star break hitting .210/.234/.317, but then returned with an open stance and higher hand position and posted a .299/.315/.530 line the rest of the season. The changes more than doubled his barrel rate and lifted his hard-hit rate by nine points, placing him among the league's best in the second half. He cooled off in September, but the quality of his contact matched July and earlier levels, with August marking his best month by hard-hit rate. While his month-to-month splits raise questions about the true effect of the adjustments, the second-half surge has turned mounting frustration into tempered optimism.

name: Otto Lopez
season_outlook: Lopez was mostly a high-average speed threat for the Marlins in 2024, but he added a bit more pop in 2025 at the expense of his batting average. He batted .246 in 143 games last season -- down from .270 -- and totaled 15 home runs and 15 steals, compared to six homers and 20 stolen bases over 161 fewer plate appearances in 2024. The improved power may not stick around since Lopez still didn't consistently make hard contact, but double-digit homers with 20-plus steals is a realistic expectation at this point, though the other counting stats are likely to be limited. Lopez opened 2025 as Miami's primary second baseman but was shifted to shortstop midseason, and his strong defense at both positions will help to keep him in the lineup.

name: JJ Wetherholt
season_outlook: The Cardinals' top prospect entering 2026, Wetherholt would make a lot of sense for them in their Opening Day lineup, considering their shift to a rebuild and February’s trade of Brendan Donovan. Wetherholt has torn through three minor-league levels in just 14 months (and 138 games), batting a robust .314/.416/.562 with 10 homers and nine steals in 47 season-concluding games for Triple-A Memphis last year. He has an elite plate approach, which should ease his transition to the majors and make him particularly attractive in points leagues. He's a dynasty building block and, if he breaks camp as the team's second baseman or shortstop as expected, would be a top Rookie of the Year candidate.

name: Brent Rooker
season_outlook: Fresh off a career year in 2024 and with his team moving to one of baseball's most hitter-friendly environments in Sacramento last season, Rooker seemed primed to potentially take another step forward. Come year's end, his 2025 had an eerie 2023 look to it, albeit with some key improvements. He traded some of his power for contact, with his fly-ball rate plummeting by 4% but his contact rate improving by roughly the same margin. The end result probably prevents Rooker from winning future home run crowns, but for as long as he calls Sutter Health Park his home, he'll be good for at least his 2025 numbers, if not better.

name: Christian Walker
season_outlook: The Astros thought they had solved their problems at first base when they signed Walker to a three-year, $60 million contract in December of 2024, but he mostly ended up just being the club's latest headache. The veteran first baseman struggled out of the gate with a .210/.273/.357 slash line through the first two months of the season, and he was never quite able to dig out of that hole. Walker showed signs of life in July and August with an .831 OPS, but that type of production was the expectation for the full season, not just two months. He still launched 27 home runs -- his fourth straight year with at least 26 -- and had respectable RBI (88) and run (72) totals, but the lack of consistency was a major issue. Walker is a decent candidate to bounce back in 2026, with his power and run production providing a solid floor despite the fact he's coming off a disappointing season.

name: Roman Anthony
season_outlook: Baseball's consensus top prospect at the time of his June 2025 debut, Anthony put forth a promising, albeit far from eye-popping, three months of production before an oblique strain brought his year to a premature close. During that time, he managed the majors' second-best Statcast hard hit rate (60.4%) and eighth-best OBP (.396), though he put the ball on the ground too often (50.6% rate). The seeds are there for Anthony to swiftly develop into a fantasy superstar, though the progression is as likely to be gradual than all at once in 2026. So long as the cost doesn't require a guarantee of the latter, he's one of the best upside picks in the early-to-mid rounds of your draft.

name: Ryan O'Hearn
season_outlook: O’Hearn has carved out a “strong side of a straight platoon” role over the past three seasons, batting .280/.346/.445 against righties in that time, which makes him one of the more useful late-round picks in fantasy leagues that allow daily transactions. His move to Pittsburgh, and pitcher-friendly PNC Park, does lower his prospective number of actionable matchups somewhat, but he’s someone to keep in mind as you round out your roster.

name: Steven Kwan
season_outlook: Kwan could not sustain the power gains from the prior season, though he still reached double-digit home runs for the second straight year. The 2024 spike was driven by more flyballs, and while he elevated the ball even more last season, the contact quality was not as strong, resulting in fewer homers and a career-low BABIP. Only three qualified hitters put the ball in play more often, keeping Kwan a steady batting average contributor, and he matched his career high with 21 steals. His durability also returned, as he missed just six games after appearing in only 122 the year before. Ignore the dip in power and draft Kwan for average and speed, with any home runs coming as a bonus.

name: Josh Naylor
season_outlook: Among the most shocking outcomes in fantasy baseball history has to be Naylor's 30 stolen bases last season, in a year where his Statcast sprint speed placed in the 3rd percentile -- third!!! Kudos to a guy who has one of the better success rates among base stealers historically, and is never afraid to run, but his 19 steals across 54 games once he was traded to Dan Wilson's Mariners is simply unsustainable (even though Wilson is one of the game's most aggressive managers on that front). And all this overshadows what are pretty good hitting metrics and balanced platoon splits, meaning Naylor is in about as good a place for a 20/20 potential season as he could ask. He's an underrated, early-round potential pick in rotisserie leagues, and is an early-to-mid rounder in points leagues.

name: Bo Bichette
season_outlook: After a miserable, injury-marred 2024, Bichette rebounded last season with the same kind of elite-contact, line drive-oriented approach he exhibited during his 2021-23 peak -- only to see his regular season (and early postseason) interrupted by yet another injury, this time a knee sprain. It rekindled the durability question, which has sapped almost all of the above-average speed he once possessed. The Mets are banking on Bichette's per-game hitting numbers, which were excellent across five months, as being more representative of his skill set, and we tend to agree. Still, we'd understand if his injury risk causes you to balk at the cost of a top-50 overall pick.

name: Bryan Reynolds
season_outlook: After four straight seasons of above-average production, Reynolds slipped to slightly below the norm, driven by a spike in his strikeout rate and a BABIP that didn't align with his batted-ball mix. He failed to gain the typical batting average boost that comes with more groundballs and line drives. His batting average dropped 30 points from the prior season, while his slugging finished 45 points below 2024. That said, his xBA was actually one point higher, and his xSLG was only 25 points short of the previous year. The downturn extended to the running game, as Reynolds went just 3-for-5 in steal attempts after going a combined 22-for-25 over the prior two seasons. Just 31 years old, Reynolds appears capable of a rebound if his strikeout and flyball rates move back toward earlier levels.

name: Tyler Soderstrom
season_outlook: Soderstrom got off to a scorching start in 2025. Through three weeks, he was the MLB leader in home runs and was fourth among hitters in fantasy points. He ultimately delivered a modest breakthrough campaign, despite the arrival of eventual Rookie of the Year Nick Kurtz shifting him to left field in late April. While Soderstrom couldn’t maintain that lofty pace, he maintained solid power numbers, held his own against left-handed pitchers and had better road numbers away from hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park than at home. He’ll need to add more loft to his swing to take another big step forward from here, but as a 24-year-old in a good home environment for bats, he’s well worth a mid-to-late round fantasy pick.

name: Ernie Clement
season_outlook: Clement ended up being a key contributor for the Blue Jays throughout 2025, batting .277 with 35 doubles, 50 RBI and 83 runs in 157 games. He hit just nine home runs and stole six bags, both of which were drops from 2024 when he recorded 12 apiece. He makes a ton of contact and had low strikeout and walk rates (10.4 percent and 4.7 percent, respectively). Clement played in at least 29 games at third base, second base and shortstop while also making 15 appearances at first, which is more playing time than a utility player usually gets. Clement doesn't really profile as a true lineup regular, and he could be pushed out of a starting role, depending who else the Blue Jays sign this winter. He can have some deep-league appeal due to the high average, run potential and defensive versatility but likely won't get enough volume to be a reliable fantasy contributor.

name: George Springer
season_outlook: Springer found the Fountain of Youth in 2025 with a .309 average, 32 homers and 18 steals across 140 regular-season games. He also tied for ninth in MLB in runs scored with 106 while often setting the table for a potent Blue Jays lineup. The incredible resurgence continued into October, with Springer posting an .899 OPS and four more homers during Toronto's run to the pennant. At 35 years old, Springer spent the majority of his time at designated hitter, though he still qualifies in the outfield. Prior to last season, Springer was in steady decline, bottoming out in 2024. However, in 2025 he looked nothing at all like a player on his last gasp in the major leagues. The DH tag should in theory help preserve his health in his late-30s.

name: Rafael Devers
season_outlook: Devers has been a star since he hit the scene in 2017, but 2025 saw him come to a career crossroads due to an unwillingness to make a much-needed defensive change which ultimately led to him being traded from Boston midseason. The turmoil began in camp and carried over to the regular season when Devers began the season 2-for-27 with 15 strikeouts. He recovered nicely and went onto hit .289/.416/.528 before the infighting became too much and he was sent to San Francisco. The move to Oracle Park and the National League had an impact on his numbers as he hit .236/.347/.480 the rest of the season, but with 20 of his 35 homers after the trade. By season's end, the counting category production was where it should have been even as his average suffered. The now 1B/DH is still an early-round selection.

name: Luis Arraez
season_outlook: A throwback type thanks to his elite-contact, batting average-but-minimal-pop hitting style, Arraez was a relative disappointment in 2025. He fell 12 points short of what would’ve been a fourth consecutive National League batting title, and the Padres struggled to find defensive positions at which to slot him due to his deficiencies in that regard. Teams might’ve seen similar issues with Arraez when considering him as a free-agent target, though the Giants ultimately saw enough in him to make him their everyday second baseman and probable No. 2 hitter. He’ll remain an underrated points league pick in that role, perhaps even from within the top 100 tier, while stabilizing roto teams’ batting averages.

name: Salvador Perez
season_outlook: Perez once again fended off Father Time as he continues to outproduce catchers more than 10 years his junior. Ignore his lowest batting average since 2018; his xBA was his best since 2020, and his xSLG was tops since 2021. His strikeout, barrel and hard-hit rates were all better than in recent seasons. His bat speed dropped a tick, but after all, it was his 14th season, much of that time spent squatting his burly 6-foot-3 frame behind home plate. The Royals are doing a good job keeping the veteran fresh by frequently rotating him through first base and designated hitter. The catcher position continues to be replenished with promising young talent, but last season's perceived slide and another year of mileage could depress the price enough to make betting on Perez remaining a top-10 backstop worthwhile.

name: Vinnie Pasquantino
season_outlook: Better injury luck and some slight elevation in his launch angle fueled a major breakthrough for Pasquantino last season, as he became the first left handed-hitting Royal with a 30-HR, 100-RBI campaign since George Brett 40 years earlier. While Pasquantino's underlying contact-quality metrics hinted some good fortune was involved -- his Barrel and hard-hit rates placed in the 65th and 57th percentiles -- his prospects for a repeat were helped by the Royals' January announcement that they'll shrink Kauffman Stadium's power-alley dimensions for 2026. He's a prime-age first baseman with elite contact skills and should be targeted in the early-to-mid rounds of any draft.

name: Matt Chapman
season_outlook: Heralded for his defense at third base, Chapman does not hit for a high batting average (career .240) but has been above a .750 OPS in all but one of his nine big-league seasons to date. Chapman has been a consistent contributor with 20-plus homers four of the past five years, reaching 21 with the Giants last season despite multiple trips to the IL with a hand injury he first suffered while diving back into the first-base bag in June. Chapman has added steals in the years since MLB limited the number of throws to first base among other rule changes to facilitate the running game, and he's now well established as a net positive on both sides of the ball. The two-time Platinum Glover projects to continue batting fourth or fifth on a daily basis for San Francisco, health permitting.

name: Teoscar Hernandez
season_outlook: The Dodgers repeated as champions, but Hernandez did not contribute to the same level during the 2025 regular season as the Regression Monster caught up to him. He spent time on the injured list in May with an adductor strain and also missed time after fouling a pitch off his foot. Ultimately, he lost eight homers, 10 RBI and seven steals from his 2024 totals, along with more than 100 points in OPS. The slugger was still a net positive but only slightly due to his deteriorating defense in right field. With Shohei Ohtani taking up the DH spot, Hernandez has to play the outfield to remain in the Los Angeles lineup. For now, he projects to remain a regular, but his poor defense at 33 years old leaves open some downside risk in regards to playing time.

name: Wyatt Langford
season_outlook: Oblique issues sent Langford to the IL on three separate occasions in 2025, obstructing what was otherwise a solid step forward by him in his sophomore season. He was one of 16 players with at least 22 home runs and stolen bases, and he reflected noticeable gains in terms of Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates, while finishing in the 85th percentile in line-drive rate. Now 24, Langford could be ready to come into his own, though better luck in the health department will certainly play a part. He's an early-to-mid round pick with upside in all formats.

name: Eugenio Suarez
season_outlook: Suarez's "HR or nothing" approach at the plate paid its biggest dividends in 2025, from his four-homer game in late April, to his season-ending career bests of 49 HR, 118 RBI, 40.9% fly ball and 47.6% hard-hit rates. Shifting his swing in that direction over the years has put him at an elevated risk of low batting averages, however, as well as peaks and valleys in his performance. That's not the kind of profile that seems likely to age well, and Suarez will play most of 2026 at 34 years of age. Expect some regression in the power department, though he should still put the ball over the fence frequently enough to remain a top-10 fantasy third baseman.

name: Kazuma Okamoto
season_outlook: After hitting 232 home runs across a seven-year span (2018-24) in Japan, Okamoto suffered an elbow injury in a collision at first base, limiting him to a career-low 77 games. Ah, but what productive games they were! He hit .322/.411/.581 and made contact 87% of the time -- all of those career-best rates -- which bodes well for a smooth transition to the U.S. game. Okamoto figures to slide in at third base for the Blue Jays, where he'll benefit from hitting in the middle-to-lower portion of their deep lineup. As is the case with any Japanese hitter, his range of outcomes is wide due to the adjustment period required, but he's a well-rounded hitter who brings a lot of fantasy upside in the late rounds.

name: Brendan Donovan
season_outlook: One of baseball's best bat handlers -- he's one of four players with at least 85% contact and 27.5% line-drive rates and 500 plate appearances over the last two seasons combined -- Donovan's skill set makes him one of the most underrated points-league players, even if he's only a back-of-your-roster utility type in rotisserie formats. Traded to the Mariners in February, he’ll likely serve as their leadoff man against right-handed pitchers, giving him more of a matchup lean in shallow mixed leagues but also boosting his run-scoring potential on the whole. Donovan's ceiling isn't especially high, but he's likely to deliver another top-100 fantasy point total in 2026.

name: Gleyber Torres
season_outlook: Torres enjoyed a resurgent campaign in his first season with Detroit, making his first All-Star team since 2019, though he regressed hard in the second half with a .659 OPS compared to an .812 OPS before the break. After the Tigers were eliminated from the postseason, Torres underwent sports hernia surgery. He was cleared for full activity in December. Despite the late slide, the Tigers extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which Torres accepted. With that, the 29-year-old will return to second base and presumably to the top third of the order after batting almost exclusively first or second under manager A.J. Hinch last season. While Torres does not pack the power or speed to be especially exciting for fantasy purposes, he does enough to be worthwhile in most formats.

name: Ivan Herrera
season_outlook: An elbow issue that required offseason surgery bumped Herrera off catcher and to DH around midseason, at a point in 2025 too early for him to log the requisite time to maintain eligibility behind the plate. It's a shame, as his skill set -- solid contact, plate discipline skills and pop, as well as aggressiveness on the bases -- is intriguing for fantasy purposes from a catcher, but much more commonplace from a DH (a position that lets you use anyone). The Cardinals claim that Herrera should be able to return to catching duties in 2026, but his defensive limitations there might slow that process. Considering he'd have a top-10 ceiling at catcher, take a flier on him late and keep your fingers crossed.

name: Willy Adames
season_outlook: Adames entered his first season with the Giants facing two uncertainties: how the move to Oracle Park would affect his bat, and whether his running game would hold up. The shift from hitter-friendly American Family Field to a park that suppresses offense showed up in his surface numbers, but not in his skills. His 108 wRC+ matched his final three years in Milwaukee, indicating his performance held steady after park adjustment, even if his 2025 wOBA dipped. His barrel and hard-hit rates ticked up slightly, while his strikeout rate reached a three-year high, keeping his batting average volatile despite power that plays anywhere. He attempted fewer steals, largely reflecting team philosophy. Overall, Adames continues to profile as a mid-tier shortstop.

name: Jeremy Pena
season_outlook: Pena put together his first career All-Star season at 27 years old, hitting .304 with 17 homers and 20 steals across 125 games with the Astros, but injuries derailed him late. The shortstop missed the entire month of July with a fractured rib after being hit by a pitch and ended the season on the IL with an oblique injury. The biggest area of growth was in the BA department as he finished top five in MLB, though Statcast puts him at a .273 xBA based on the quality and amount of contact. Assuming full health after an offseason of rest, Pena will return to an everyday role in Houston where he has genuinely moved the needle since breaking in a few years back. Regression to the rate numbers seems likely, but it's reasonable to think Pena could still find another level with his counting stats in 2026.

name: Konnor Griffin
season_outlook: Widely regarded as the top prospect in all of baseball, Griffin's skill set is regarded so highly that he has generated some chatter that he could break camp with the Pirates and perhaps even win the NL  Rookie of the Year Award, despite only one year's pro experience under his belt. What a debut year it was, as he hit 21 homers, stole 65 bases, hit .333/.415/.527, played solid shortstop and performed equally well across three competitive levels through Double-A. Griffin is the kind of future-MVP-caliber prospect that dynasty league managers should build around. Redraft managers should scoop him up instantly upon his promotion. If you've got space to stash him, a realistic ETA in Pittsburgh might be before mid-season.

name: Yainer Diaz
season_outlook: Diaz's wRC+ declined for the second straight season despite a gain in power. Over the prior two years, his batting average closely tracked his xBA, but last season he finished 16 points below expected, driven largely by an unusually low line-drive BABIP. He also posted a career-low hard-hit rate, working against batting average. Added loft did push his barrel rate to a career high, and he paired that with the lowest strikeout rate of his career. Diaz grades as a below-average defender, so reversing the offensive slide will be important if he is to remain among the most heavily used backstops after his 567 plate appearances ranked sixth among catcher-eligible players last season. More line drives falling in would help, but he also needs to hit the ball with more authority and with greater selectivity.

name: Agustin Ramirez
season_outlook: Ramirez arrived in Miami three weeks into the season and, as is all the rage these days, saw near-everyday time between catcher and DH to fuel what was the third-most fantasy points by any catcher-eligible player from that point forward. Though he cooled over the season's final three months, batting only .212 with a .633 OPS, his fantasy value was buoyed by his 15 stolen bases over that time. His well-rounded game, and his penchant for contact, gives him a good shot at another top-10 catcher season, if not a step forward in 2026.

name: Marcus Semien
season_outlook: Heading into the 2025 season, Semien had been a model of reliability playing in the fifth-most games since he came into the league in 2015 while playing in three organizations with solid-to-spectacular production from his middle-infield positions. However, age appeared to catch up with him in 2025 as he had the worst season of his career at the plate which was eventually ended by a foot injury resulting from a foul ball. The Rangers, reticent to spend on the free-agent market, decided to trade Semien to the Mets for Brandon Nimmo, which could be a boon for a fully healthy Semien. He should now find himself nestled between Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto at the top of the Mets lineup providing him both ample RBI chances as well as plenty of run-scoring opportunities. He deserves one more chance from fantasy managers.

name: Michael Busch
season_outlook: Busch is coming off a tremendous sophomore season which saw him flex his power to another level while improving his strikeout rate five full percentage points. Busch hit 30 of his 34 homers against righties and was quite neutralized by lefties all season, and he found road parks to be more conducive to his homers with 21 of the 34 coming away from Wrigley Field. Busch may also be one of the few players to hit 30 or more home runs in a season during which his most common position in the batting order was leadoff, as he led off for the Cubs in 52 contests last season. Should that usage continue, Busch is likely to score more runs than he drives in, but he did still manage 90 RBI last season. If he and Ian Happ flip in the projected lineup around Nico Hoerner, Busch could drive in 100-plus.

name: Dillon Dingler
season_outlook: Dingler took over as Detroit's primary backstop in 2025 and delivered a quality rookie campaign, finishing the regular season with 13 homers, 57 RBI, 54 runs and a .278/.327/.425 slash line in 126 games. Previous No. 1 catcher Jake Rogers is coming off a second straight disappointing season at the plate, so he's likely to stick in the backup job to begin 2026. Dingler didn't walk much with just 23 free passes but had a 23.5 percent strikeout rate. Dingler also provided strong defensive value behind the plate, which will be key to maintaining playing time at a premium defensive position, though he may not quite be ready to truly play every day like the top catchers in baseball. Repeating a strong average with 10-15 homers and modest counting stats is a fair expectation in 2026.

name: Xander Bogaerts
