season_outlook: Bogaerts has been on a rather bizarre run in recent years with almost impossibly low counting stats for an established player of his caliber. A four-time All-Star and twice a 100-RBI bat during his time with the Red Sox, he has not reached even 60 RBI in a season with the Padres. Bogaerts missed time in 2024 with a fractured left shoulder and has now settled at exactly 11 homers in consecutive seasons. After transitioning to second base in 2024, Bogaerts moved back to shortstop in 2025, and with that he loses the dual eligibility that boosted his fantasy utility. The age-related decline began earlier for Bogaerts than most, but at 33 he is still a plus player for San Diego and the stolen bases help his case for continued mid-round interest.

name: Ryan Jeffers
season_outlook: Jeffers traded power for average last season -- 12 homers for 40 points in BA, specifically. He improved his chase rate in 2025 and started to take off in the second half (.297) before a concussion sidelined him for a stretch in September. The backstop returned during the final week, gaining a clean bill of health heading into the offseason. It would be nice if he could now add power back to the profile, but regardless of how the stats have been distributed, at the end of the day Jeffers' bat has been above league average three years running. While the team context is a slight drawback, he projects to retain the lion's share of the workload in Minnesota, which gives him an edge over other second-catcher options.

name: Josh Jung
season_outlook: Jung was limited to just 46 games in 2024 due to a wrist injury, but he was able to stay mostly healthy last season and played in a career-high 131 contests. Unfortunately for fantasy managers, his offensive production still took a hit, and he finished 2025 with a .251 average, 14 homers and a career-low .390 slugging percentage. The Rangers demoted Jung to the minors for a few weeks over the summer, and he did fare a bit better the rest of the way with a .732 OPS, but he was still far from a consistent contributor. The power potential is obvious given the 23 homers that Jung launched as a rookie in 2023, but injuries and inconsistency have made him a volatile fantasy option with a seemingly low floor.

name: Jackson Holliday
season_outlook: "Well?! We're waiting!" It might feel like forever to fantasy managers, but it's important to remember that Holliday, the No. 1 pick of the 2022 Draft and consensus No. 1 prospect entering his 2024 MLB debut season, is still only 22 years old and just 427 professional games removed from high school. Not all prospects blossom immediately, and perhaps he's one of those who takes baby steps to get there. Holliday's metrics were so-so at best in his first full big-league campaign in 2025, but he did greatly improve his patience (95th percentile chase rate) and contact (80th percentile rate) during the season's second half, and he showed hints of future five-category rotisserie potential. That said, a fractured right hamate bone suffered in February will cost him important spring training time and likely land him on the IL to start the season. Holliday is still a high-upside middle-round pick, but picking him requires a bit of a leap of faith.

name: Jose Caballero
season_outlook: The AL’s leading base stealer in both of the last two seasons, Caballero has the look of a single-category, roto-angled standout -- until you look closer. He improved his plate approach and the resulting walk rate (12.7%) last year, demonstrated above-average defense at five different positions (while also appearing in a sixth, in center field) and gave the Yankees reasonable cause to let him push Anthony Volpe for their starting shortstop job this spring. Caballero’s skill set indeed is better suited for roto play, where he’s a strong mid-round pick for his steals, but a standout March could make him a potential breakout candidate.

name: Bryson Stott
season_outlook: Stott put together a respectable if unspectacular campaign as the Phillies' regular second baseman in 2025, hitting 13 home runs and stealing 24 bags across 147 regular-season games. He sat occasionally against left-handed pitching and did little against southpaws when given the opportunity with a .575 OPS and one homer in 123 PA without the platoon edge. A plus on defense, Stott figures to remain Trea Turner's double-play partner in Philadelphia for the foreseeable future despite his shortcomings. Citizens Bank Park is hitter friendly and Stott isn't asked to carry much of the load offensively, for better or worse. Manager Rob Thomson experimented with Stott in the leadoff spot last season but eventually settled on him being a lower-third bat even against right-handed pitching.

name: Brandon Marsh
season_outlook: The Phillies have talked about wanting to utilize Marsh as an everyday outfielder rather than a platoon player since acquiring him in 2022, but his continued struggles against left-handed pitching (.577 OPS in 2025) have essentially made that impossible. The good news is that he continues to crush righties and posted a .300/.356/.482 slash line against them last season. His production on the basepaths dropped significantly with just seven steals after he posted a career-high 19 in 2024, and 11 home runs marked his lowest total since 2022 while his 43 RBI and 59 runs were also underwhelming. Marsh's ratios continue to be strong, but the lack of volume significantly caps his counting stats and limits his upside in most formats.

name: Isaac Paredes
season_outlook: Paredes' 2025 season can best be summed up by what could have been. The third baseman hit 20 homers in 102 games while being forced to miss two full months with an acute hamstring tear that initially looked like a season-ending injury. Paredes' extreme pull and flyball approach are an ideal fit for his home stadium, yet just 11 of his 20 home runs came at Daikin Park. Paredes previously hit 31 homers around the challenges of Tropicana Field and the changing of the dimensions in Baltimore in 2023, so we know what a full season of his approach is capable of, but that same approach also leaves him quite susceptible to batting average risk, because his batted balls that do not leave the yard are either cans of corn or routine groundball outs to the left side due to his slow foot speed. He might hit 40 home runs in 2026, but he may also struggle to hit .240.

name: Jonathan Aranda
season_outlook: Aranda's counting stats from 2025 don't really stand out on the surface as he finished with 14 homers, 59 RBI and 56 runs, but he remarkably did most of that damage before the end of July when a collision with Giancarlo Stanton sidelined him for nearly two full months. Overall for the year, he delivered a .316/.393/.489 slash line in 106 games, priming him for a full breakout if he can stay healthy in 2026. Aranda's batted-ball metrics ranked among the best in the league, so there shouldn't be much worry about that elite performance being luck driven. He also returned for three games at the end of the regular season and went 4-for-12 with two long balls, eliminating concern about injury carryover. Aranda should bat in the heart of Tampa Bay's batting order in 2026, and fantasy managers are likely going to have to invest heavily to nab him on draft day.

name: Caleb Durbin
season_outlook: Durbin gave Milwaukee and its fans an exciting immediate return on investment from trading Devin Williams in the offseason. Durbin leveraged a successful showing in the Arizona Fall League to earn a mid-April promotion to Milwaukee and never looked back. Durbin had the fifth-lowest strikeout rate for all batters with at least 500 plate appearances in 2025 and was a pest at the bottom of the Milwaukee lineup as a tough out at the plate while also being tough on the bases, stealing 18 bases in 24 attempts. Durbin will be hard pressed to hit more homers in 2026, but there is certainly room for batting average growth with better batted-ball fortunes and stolen bases with the accompanying improvement to his on-base percentage. The skills are there for a .280 average and 30-plus steals with better luck. Following his trade to the Red Sox, he'll likely start at third base.

name: Giancarlo Stanton
season_outlook: Stanton didn't debut for the Yankees in 2025 until mid-June due to tendinitis in both elbows, but his presence was worth the wait as he posted 24 home runs and a .944 OPS, which was his best mark since his MVP campaign in 2017. He played in just 77 games but still provided plenty of run production with 66 RBI, though his actual runs total (36) was unsurprisingly much lower given his awful sprint speed. A 34.3 percent strikeout rate was the highest of Stanton's career, but he continues to hit the ball as hard as anyone in baseball. Expecting a repeat of that production over a larger sample wouldn't be wise, but Stanton has clubbed 24-plus homers each of the past five seasons and seems likely to do so again in 2026, even as he enters his age-36 season.

name: Willson Contreras
season_outlook: The Cardinals moved Contreras from catcher to first base last offseason, but the defensive move didn't bring significant change at the plate as he posted a .257/.344/.447 slash line with 20 home runs, 80 RBI and 70 runs in 135 games. A .791 OPS ended up being his worst mark since 2021, and that was largely fueled by his 8.2 percent walk rate, which was nearly five points worse than his 2024 mark. Being traded from the rebuilding Cardinals to the Red Sox in December should provide Contreras with the potential for more run production in 2026, especially since Fenway Park is more hitter friendly to right-handed bats than Busch Stadium. Contreras has a pretty well established floor with an average of 20 home runs, 59 RBI, 60 runs and a .252 batting average across the past five seasons, so he's a fairly safe mid-tier fantasy target.

name: Colson Montgomery
season_outlook: Now, where did that come from? Montgomery arrived in Chicago in early July and quickly went on an uncharacteristic power surge. Over a 37-game span a few weeks after his recall, he hit 18 home runs, matching his entire 2024 total across 130 minor-league games. And that's not to say that he can't do it again, as he had strong underlying hard-contact metrics, but his 17.2% HR/FB rate, which was eighth-highest in the league from his debut date forward, hints that there'll be some pullback. Montgomery might need to improve his plate approach in order to take another step forward in 2026. As it is, he's a late-round pick for mixed-league play.

name: Jac Caglianone
season_outlook: Caglianone had one of the more disappointing rookie seasons in 2025, posting the worst batting average (.157) and OPS (.532) among those with at least 200 plate appearances, while sporting one of the league's worst chase rates. But, to be fair, he was also only a little over a year removed from being a two-way player at Florida, with only 95 games of minor-league experience focusing on hitting alone at the time. Caglianone did flash gaudy bat speed and Barrel metrics, and the 20 homers he hit in 66 minor-league games underscore his massive potential in that department. The Royals' decision to shrink the outfield dimensions at Kauffman Stadium should also help him. If Caglianone is swinging well in Cactus League play, make sure to scoop him up late in the hopes he's ready to break through at age 23.

name: Samuel Basallo
season_outlook: Seemingly blocked at his primary position at the MLB  level by Adley Rutschman, Basallo parlayed .270/.377/.589 rates and 23 homers in 76 games for Triple-A Norfolk into his first opportunity with the Orioles once Rutschman's oblique issues resurfaced in mid-August. Basallo would struggle through a too-aggressive approach at the plate, batting only .165 while striking out over 25% of the time, but he flashed decent pop and was a plenty serviceable backstop. He's expected to serve in a catcher/DH partnership with Rutschman in 2026, from which both will hinder the other's playing time somewhat, but also from which both could be fantasy-relevant and even prospective top-10 positional values. The long-term sky's the limit with this kid.

name: Trent Grisham
season_outlook: Grisham had an improbable 2025 season which saw him double his previous career high of 17 home runs, hitting 34 for the Yankees in his final year before free agency. He was one of the early advocates for the torpedo bat style, but that alone did not fuel this breakout power season as much as Grisham's overall deliberate approach to hitting. He is very patient at the plate and went hunting for fastballs early in counts, and often found them with 21 of his 34 homers coming from fastballs. Before you give Yankee Stadium's short porch too much credit, understand Grisham's home OPS was 200 points lower than it was on the road and he hit just 13 of his 34 home runs at Yankee Stadium last season. Grisham took the qualifying offer to firm up his free agency vitae with the thought Yankee Stadium cannot possibly punish him two consecutive seasons.

name: Brooks Lee
season_outlook: Lee got his first full season in the majors in 2025, and much like the Twins as a team, it was largely a disappointing campaign. He played in 139 games and clubbed 16 homers with three steals, 64 RBI and 50 runs while posting an underwhelming .236/.285/.370 slash line. He split playing time between shortstop, second base and third base and will have eligibility at all three positions in 2026, but he's expected to work primarily at shortstop following the departure of Carlos Correa to Houston. Lee often hit for a high average in the minors but otherwise didn't stand out much statistically. He doesn't offer much speed and likely doesn't have much power upside beyond what he's already shown, so his fantasy ceiling is fairly limited, though he should get plenty of volume on the rebuilding Twins.

name: Gabriel Moreno
season_outlook: Injuries again marred Moreno's season, as he appeared in fewer than 100 games for the second straight year. He was batting .270/.324/.414 in mid-June when he was finally placed on the IL after being hit in the hand two weeks earlier. The fractured finger sidelined him for more than two months, and after returning he posted an impressive .311/.397/.466 line over 30 games. For the season, he set new personal bests in barrel and hard-hit rate while hitting more flyballs to drive power. That came at the cost of a higher strikeout rate, though it remained well below average. Moreno's typically strong defense graded as league average, but he played fewer games behind the plate, especially down the stretch when he often served as the DH. It's unclear how much of last season's gains will carry over, and durability remains a concern.

name: Jorge Soler
season_outlook: Soler was limited to 82 games in 2025 due to back issues, which resulted in two trips to the injured list and cost him the final two months of the season. The veteran slugger wasn't particularly productive when available, finishing with 12 home runs, 34 RBI, 31 runs and a .215/.293/.387 slash line in 314 plate appearances. Soler is now entering his age-34 season, so the recurring back issues in 2025 could spell trouble moving forward, especially since he already wasn't the most consistent of hitters. Still, he's just two seasons removed from clubbing 36 homers for Miami, and he played in at least 137 games in both 2023 and 2024. Soler can't be fully written off despite the age and injury concerns.

name: Carter Jensen
season_outlook: Regarded as the Royals’ catcher of the future, or at least a catcher/DH partner for Salvador Perez until the latter’s retirement, Jensen has an unusually sound combination of plate discipline and pop -- or at least it’s unusual for a backstop. He received a September cup of coffee with the Royals, hitting three homers with a .941 OPS in his 20 games, and he now figures to grab a similar role with the big club to begin 2026. Jensen has one of the highest ceilings among young catchers, and the promise of DH at-bats boosts his appeal in the runs/RBI categories. If he looks likely to break camp with the team, he could be a top-10 fantasy catcher right from the start.

name: Carlos Correa
season_outlook: Correa should be projected for zero steals, with his last one coming in 2019. He began last season with the Twins but was dealt back to Houston at the trade deadline after producing a .267/.319/.386 line over 95 games. Feeling rejuvenated, Correa improved to .290/.355/.430 over 51 games with the Astros. The only differences in his approach were a bit more patience and more flyballs, perhaps due to seeing the inviting and familiar Crawford Boxes. Correa hit seven homers in four months with the Twins, and then clubbed six in two months back with the Astros. New this season is dual eligibility at third base and shortstop, which will be useful since he profiles as a corner or middle infielder in mixed leagues. The upside is minimal but the added flexibility helps his appeal.

name: Ramon Laureano
season_outlook: One of the few things that went right for the disappointing 2025 Orioles, Laureano performed as he had in his early days in Oakland for four months, then maintained that level of production following a midseason trade to the Padres, before a fractured finger ended his year in the final week. With his boosted power metrics and balanced platoon splits, he earned a place as the Padres' starting left fielder and heart-of-the-order hitter, the latter boosting his RBI potential. Everything in Laureano's 2025 metrics supports his ability to repeat the effort, making him a solid late-rounder for fantasy play.

name: Andres Gimenez
season_outlook: Gimenez was traded from the Guardians to the Blue Jays last winter, but he continued on his downward trajectory and finished the 2025 regular season with a .210/.285/.313 slash line in 101 games. He totaled seven home runs, 12 stolen bases, 35 RBI and 39 runs, with the steals production being especially notable coming off two consecutive 30-theft campaigns. Two month-long stints on the injured list due to quadriceps and ankle injuries may have played a role in that reduction. It's worth noting that his sprint speed did drop almost a full tick to 28 mph. Regardless, Gimenez doesn't offer broad fantasy appeal, though he could be a viable single-category contributor with a rebound on the basepaths, which wouldn't be a major surprise in his age-27 campaign. His elite defense should help to keep him in the lineup even if the offensive struggles persist.

name: Francisco Alvarez
season_outlook: Alvarez has had an interesting past 12-18 months. The catcher suffered a hamate bone fracture in early March which delayed the start to his 2025 season, and then he was demoted to Triple-A after a slow .236/.319/.333 start which included struggles behind the plate. He returned with a vengeance just after the break and hit .276/.360/.561, reminding everyone of his potential even while playing through a sprained UCL in his right thumb. That UCL injury means he has needed surgery to repair the UCLs in both of his hands as well as the hamate bone fracture in the past year. His offseason preparation may once again be affected, but those second-half numbers remind us of the tremendous upside in this young man. The balance between risk and reward is the big question.

name: J.T. Realmuto
season_outlook: Few active players have followed a smoother career aging curve than Realmuto, who at 34 years old last season saw predictable dips in his power and bat-speed metrics, but not nearly enough to dissuade the Phillies from bringing him back on a three-year, $45 million deal. They recognize his worth on the defensive side (important in fantasy because of how it props up his playing time), as well as his above-average skills with the bat as well as on the basepaths. Realmuto is no longer the fantasy star behind the plate that he was, but he was a top-15 player at the position in both roto and points leagues last year. That’s a threshold he can certainly reach again in 2026.

name: Jordan Westburg
season_outlook: Westburg's output closely matched the prior season, though injuries again played a central role. A broken hand limited him to 107 games in 2024 and wiped out much of the second half, while last year brought a late-April hamstring injury sidelining him for almost six weeks, followed by a mid-August ankle sprain that cost him another month. The skill gains he showed before the 2024 injury didn't carry over, and his plate discipline has slipped from his minor-league days, with a walk rate just under five percent across the past two seasons. Improved health and greater patience could allow more of his power to surface. He isn't an aggressive base stealer by nature, and the injuries further reduced his running. Limited to 85 games, Westburg also came up three games shy of second-base eligibility in most formats.

name: Cam Smith
season_outlook: Smith was one of the stories of spring training last year when his long-shot bid to make Houston's Opening Day roster was successful, but the harsh realities of Major League Baseball eventually set in. The third-baseman-turned-outfielder hit the skids in the summer months and finished with a .154/.247/.242 line in the second half. GM Dana Brown acknowledged after the 2025 season that Smith could require more time back on the farm, pointing to the need for greater consistency. It wasn't all bad as Smith had his moments, including a two-homer game in April, but the way his rookie year ended suggests a reset may be necessary. The upside is still there long term for the 2024 first-round pick whom the Astros acquired from the Cubs as part of the return for Kyle Tucker.

name: Spencer Steer
season_outlook: Throughout 2025, Steer was held back by some upper-back issues which never put on him on the injured list but did hamper his ability to drive the ball with authority on a consistent basis. Steer once again hit 20-plus homers for a third consecutive season, and he was pacing to set a new career high if not limited by the nagging injury. He lost nearly 90 plate appearances from the previous two seasons both due to injury and the club giving Sal Stewart some extra time at first base down the stretch. It was surprising to see Steer's stolen-base production fall off as much as it did in 2025 with Terry Francona's lead foot taking over the running game, but that too could easily return if Steer is 100 percent healthy for 2026. The 2023 season was a great one for him with an .820 OPS, but Steer has yet to replicate that level of production.

name: Carson Kelly
season_outlook: Kelly got off to a scorching start last season, batting .361/.500/.820 with eight home runs through the Cubs’ first 36 games, before regression grabbed hold and restored him to borderline top-25 fantasy catcher status. It’s not that that’s without value, but he’s more of a high-floor than high-ceiling type, best known for his keen eye at the plate rather than his pop. Kelly should again work in a partnership behind the plate for the Cubs, getting enough at-bats and hitting enough homers to be the kind of pick you want as your mixed-league No. 2 catcher (if your league requires one).

name: Austin Wells
season_outlook: Wells had a productive sophomore campaign for the Yankees despite some concerning trends in some of his performance indicators. Wells increased his aggressiveness at the plate, reducing his walk rate by nearly five full percentage points while his strikeout rate increased by over five percentage points. That resulted in his batting average falling further below the league average but still closer to an acceptable level for the catcher position. Wells still finished tied for fifth with 21 homers as a catcher and seventh with 71 RBI. Wells significantly improved his production against lefties, hitting six home runs while also batting .240 against southpaws. He also hit more homers on the road than at home, which goes against prevailing knowledge. His elite framing skills, as well as Ben Rice shifting to first base in 2026, should allow Wells to push for a career high in plate appearances this season.

name: Matt McLain
season_outlook: McLain has had two seasons of productive counting-category volume with the Reds, but it came around him missing the entirety of the 2024 season, and the long layoff was evident. McLain took a lot of time to round into form in 2025, as he was hitting just .178/.273/.300 heading into June with more steals (11) than extra-base hits (10) in just over 200 plate appearances. He righted the ship from there on out with a more respectable .242/.314/.367 line with 23 extra-base hits and another seven steals. The final numbers were decent for a middle infielder hitting toward the bottom of the lineup, but the 70-point dropoff in batting average was tough to carry. The rust should all be gone now and McLain projects to resume his worthwhile counting production with a boost in batting average somewhere in between his 2023 and 2025 figures.

name: Colt Keith
season_outlook: Keith has not exactly performed to the expectations set forth by his 2023 minor-league campaign, but he was more productive during his sophomore season at the big-league level in 2025. Oftentimes, players struggle to avoid the sophomore slump, yet Keith showed a more discernible eye at the plate while hitting with more power, so he appears well positioned to take another step forward in 2026. Keith's aforementioned plate discipline makes him a strong candidate to bat leadoff, which would help push his volume up. However, Keith will need to show he can do more against lefties than he has thus far in his career, because his .610 OPS against them in two seasons invites a platoon situation. His contract makes him a regular player in the lineup; what he does against lefties in 2026 will dictate whether he is promoted to an everyday role.

name: Jeff McNeil
season_outlook: McNeil will change coasts in 2026 following a December trade from the Mets to the A's. In the years since winning the batting title in 2022, McNeil has fallen well short of those same heights, and in fact has sunk to .241 over his last 934 PA. He ended his time in Queens with just six home runs at home over his final two regular seasons, compared to a combined 21 on the road in that span. Despite Citi Field suppressing his power, McNeil at least reached a double-digit homer total each of the last three years. The thump is generally lacking, but he added to his walk rate in 2025 and the move to Sacramento in 2026 provides a park boost while solidifying playing time at second base. Entering his age-34 season, McNeil carries dual eligibility (2B/OF) but is not much of a contributor on the basepaths.

name: Addison Barger
season_outlook: An adjustment to his batting stance fueled a semi-breakthrough for Barger, who hit .291/.342/.568 with 14 home runs across a 60-game stretch early in the year and reflected significant boosts in Barrel and hard-hit metrics for the full season. He'd cool off later in the year, batting .205/.270/.360 with six homers over his final 49 regular-season games, before putting forth strong showings in the ALCS and World Series. Barger's skill set is not without its limitations, as he's a weak defender and struggles against lefties, making him both a platoon and late-inning removal risk. Still, he's capable enough in the power departments to warrant a late-round pick in larger mixed fantasy leagues.

name: Masyn Winn
season_outlook: Winn's 2025 was going quite well until some knee discomfort in June revealed a slight tear in his meniscus which first required an injection and eventually led to him shutting his season down in mid-September to get a head start on the planned arthroscopic surgery. Winn had six homers heading into June but hit just three more the rest of the season, yet he was still able to steal seven bases in eight attempts on the bum knee. The injury helps explain away a lot of the traditional statistical decline Winn experienced in 2025 and gives reason to think he could be in store for improvement in 2026 assuming better luck on the health front. He may not get to 20 homers, but 20 steals with his speed and some increased opportunities on base is certainly possible. This is an underrated four-category contributor whose down 2025 offers a 2026 discount.

name: J.P. Crawford
season_outlook: Crawford posted a career-worst .202/.304/.321 slash line across 105 games in 2024, but he bounced back last season with a .265/.352/.370 line in 157 contests. He set a career high with eight stolen bases and also posted the second-highest homer total of his career (12). The run production was limited with 58 RBI and 69 runs, which is a bit disappointing given that he spent half the season batting leadoff, though he did spend the other half hitting eighth or ninth. Crawford's plate discipline remains one of his best skills at the plate, and he had an 11.5 percent walk rate and 18.7 percent strikeout rate in 2025. The production last season was pretty close to Crawford's career averages, so it's a decent barometer for his expectations in 2026.

name: Kyle Teel
season_outlook: Teel, the primary piece in the December 2024 Garrett Crochet trade, brought his intriguing combination of plate discipline, pop and smarts on the basepaths to the south side of Chicago beginning last June, putting forth one of the better beneath-the-radar campaigns among rookies. Among those with at least 250 plate appearances, his .375 OBP ranked third and his .349 wOBA sixth. From his debut date forward, he had the 12th-most fantasy points among catcher-eligibles of any experience level (140). Teel figures to again rotate with fellow youngster Edgar Quero between catcher and DH, though it's important to note that he's the more integral piece in the team's future plans. Teel could be ready for a big step forward in 2026, making him a catcher with upside to target if you're going the cheap route at the position.

name: Nolan Schanuel
season_outlook: The Angels called Schanuel up a little over a month after drafting him with the 11th overall pick in 2023, and he has been learning on the job in the years since. Not your prototypical slugger at first base, Schanuel's offensive game is built around patience, putting the ball in play and striking out at a low clip. He has totaled just 25 homers over the past two seasons even with everyday at-bats, but Schanuel was batting a healthy .274 last season before a HBP in July knocked him off course. Eventually, he landed on the IL with a bone bruise in his left wrist. The experience he has gained against big-league arms should serve him well, but Schanuel still seems to have the same limitations entering his age-24 campaign. An increase in flyball rate helped a bit with his ISO and SLG last season.

name: Jonathan India
season_outlook: The move from Cincinnati to Kansas City proved tough on India in 2025. He finished the campaign with the worst offensive numbers of his career, including a .669 OPS and nine homers in 567 PA, limping to a .194 average in the second half. The Royals are blaming his struggles partially on India moving around between second base, left field and third base, and they plan on leaving him at the keystone in 2026. Perhaps more stability in his defensive role will help his offensive production, but India is looking more and more like a player who peaked right away upon arrival in 2021 when he won NL Rookie of the Year. Any sort of bounce-back effort will likely come without steals since that aspect of his game completely vanished in his first season with the Royals.

name: Jake Burger
season_outlook: Burger was acquired by the Rangers last winter and was coming off back-to-back seasons with at least 29 home runs, but he struggled early in 2025 and missed time due to oblique, quad and wrist injuries. The slugger never fully got on track and closed out the campaign with 16 homers and a .236/.269/.419 slash line in 103 games. He walked at just a 3.3 percent clip, earning only 12 free passes in 376 plate appearances. Burger still made strong contact with a 48.5 percent hard-hit rate, so there's some hope for a power resurgence in 2026 if he can stay healthy. Burger should have a pretty regular role for the Rangers, splitting his playing time between first base and designated hitter.

name: Brenton Doyle
season_outlook: Doyle broke out in 2024 with 23 homers, 30 steals and a .763 OPS during his second MLB campaign, but he regressed significantly last season with a .233/.274/.376 slash line in 138 contests. He still provided some power and speed production with 15 long balls and 18 stolen bases, but his run production was lacking with 57 RBI and 57 runs. He made strong contact at a similar clip to 2024 with a 44.6 hard-hit rate, which provides hope for a rebound in 2026 despite the down campaign. Doyle's elite defense in center field will help him to maintain a regular spot in the lineup, and his decent floor in homers and steals make him a bounce-back candidate with a solid floor despite a poor surrounding lineup.

name: Willi Castro
season_outlook: Fantasy managers love Castro’s positional flexibility, and now they’ll love another thing about him: He’ll call Coors Field his home. Besides his defensive utility, Castro’s most marketable skill is his speed, but he’s capable enough with the bat to capitalize upon the favorable hitting environment. He’s an ideal round-out-your-roster type, able to be mixed and matched for his Coors games and against weaker starting pitchers. Just don’t expect any miracles when he’s playing on the road.

name: Jurickson Profar
season_outlook: Profar was forced to miss half the season due to a PED suspension, yet what he was able to do despite the layoff in half a season underlines why Atlanta signed him in the first place. Profar played to about a 30-20 pace, exceeding his pace of production from the prior season in his walk year in San Diego. Profar remains one of the more disciplined hitters in baseball as he is quite selective at the plate and limits his strikeouts while also accepting plenty of walks. He is one of just eight qualified hitters with a double-digit walk rate and a strikeout rate below 16 percent over the past five seasons. Profar should hit high in the Atlanta lineup and provide help in all four counting categories while hoping for better batted-ball luck in 2026 after batting .245 last season.

name: Andrew Vaughn
season_outlook: Vaughn got off to a horrific start to 2025 with the White Sox, ultimately earning himself a ticket back to Triple-A ball, then a trade to the Brewers. One Rhys Hoskins injury later and Vaughn was playing regularly in Milwaukee, generating a top-50 fantasy point total among hitters from his July 7 recall forward. Greater patience and a small adjustment to his swing contributed and, while regression is sure to strike in 2026, those changes and Milwaukee’s HR-friendly home environment should help keep Vaughn in the fantasy-relevant tier. He’s a good corner infielder for traditional mixed-league play.

name: Ezequiel Tovar
season_outlook: Tovar was hampered by injuries for much of the first half of 2025 and ended up playing in just 94 games on the year, finishing with nine home runs, five steals, 33 RBI, 44 runs and a .253/.294/.400 slash line. That line was a bit worse across the board compared to 2024, with slugging percentage being the major drop since his homer total was nearly cut in third. Despite some inconsistency, Tovar posted career bests in strikeout and walk rates (25.1 percent and 5.5 percent, respectively). The Coors Field effect has definitely been in play with a home average of .339 compared to .172 on the road. Tovar has showcased a decent floor for a mid-tier shortstop and should be able to get back around 20 long balls and double-digit steals with a healthy campaign in 2026.

name: Jasson Dominguez
season_outlook: Dominguez had a serviceable, yet far from Mickey-Mantle-esque, rookie season, though his modest second-half production (.236/.300/.318 rates) and defensive shortcomings caused the Yankees to ease off him in left field both in September and during the postseason. He's still only 23 years old and with decent power potential -- his Statcast hard-hit rate placed in the 85th percentile -- but to this point of his career, his most bankable fantasy asset is his speed. Dominguez might be ready to take another step forward in his second full season, but without a standout March, he's more of a late-round sleeper in roto leagues rather than in points formats.

name: Gavin Sheets
season_outlook: Sheets was non-tendered by the White Sox in November of 2024 and eventually landed with the Padres on a minor-league deal in February, but he ended up being one of the better success stories of 2025. He posted an .833 OPS with 11 homers in his first 51 games of the season, and although he cooled off down the stretch, he still finished the campaign with 19 home runs, 71 RBI and a .252/.317/.429 slash line in 145 contests. There's certainly a question of sustainability given the .680 OPS he posted during his four years in Chicago, but Sheets' batted-ball metrics indicate the improved results were well deserved. While his volume may be capped a bit since he's expected to continue working as a strong-side platoon player, Sheets could push for 20 homers in 2026.

name: Mark Vientos
season_outlook: A season that began with optimism after Vientos' 2024 power breakout ended in frustration, though some of it was unwarranted. His wOBA dropped by more than 50 points, but his xwOBA fell only 14 points. Some of the previous season's enthusiasm was aided by good luck, and that swung the other way last season. Vientos struck out less and hit the ball harder, but he didn't receive the same favorable results. His barrel and hard-hit rates remain well above average, but even with last season's improvement in contact, he still strikes out at a well above-average clip, and with just two career steals in four seasons, he needs power to be productive. Even if partly undeserved, Vientos' struggles last season, especially down the stretch, have his 2026 role in jeopardy. Marcus Semien is slated for second base, pushing Brett Baty back to third. Vientos could slide to first base, but Jorge Polanco was signed and is the likely fit there.

name: Anthony Volpe
season_outlook: Volpe played through a partially torn labrum in his left shoulder for much of 2025 and underwent surgery in October, which is expected to sideline him for the start of 2026. The young shortstop provided fantasy managers with solid counting stats (19 home runs, 18 steals, 72 RBI and 65 runs in 153 games), but his .212/.272/.391 slash line left a lot to be desired. Playing through the injury obviously affected Volpe's offensive performance, but it's unclear exactly how much it influenced the actual results given that his .663 OPS was nearly identical to his first two big-league campaigns. He still has 20-20 upside and appears locked in as the Yankees' primary shortstop for another year, but a delayed start to 2026 and inconsistency make Volpe a volatile fantasy target.

name: Dylan Crews
season_outlook: The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 Draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2025 rookie season, Crews put forth solid power (7 HR) and speed (11 SB) numbers across his first 45 games, though his free-swinging nature (27.7 K%) led to a miserable, .196 batting average. An oblique strain would then cost him nearly three months, after which point he delivered more of the same, but with the same 50%-plus ground ball rate that must improve for him to truly realize his full power potential. Crews should get a long look for a starting role during spring training and, as he matures, he'll at least provide a solid stolen bases total for roto managers. He's more of a profitable late-rounder there than in points leagues, though he still has a high long-term ceiling for any fantasy format.

name: Javier Baez
season_outlook: Among 2025’s most unexpected outcomes was Baez’s first-half rebound, earning him an All-Star nod. The accolades came after three straight disappointing seasons to begin his six-year, $140 million contract with the Tigers, culminating in a 2024 that was one of the league’s worst by any player. A .337 BABIP through June made it clear last year’s hot start was almost entirely fluky, and he regressed to .219/.225/.315 rates and a 29.0% strikeout rate thereafter. It paints the picture of a highly risky fantasy pick, albeit one who might see enough time and contribute just enough power and speed to warrant a late-round roto selection.

name: Brett Baty
season_outlook: Baty failed to make an impact after making the Mets' Opening Day roster last year and was demoted to Triple-A in late April, but he was called back up a couple weeks later and was able to get on track from there. The third baseman played in 130 games and posted a .254/.313/.435 slash line with 18 home runs, eight steals, 50 RBI and 53 runs. The club's roster upheaval during the offseason should give him a clear path to starting nearly every day in 2026, and he has clear 20-10 potential coming off the mini-breakout, though there's certainly some risk given he's yet to establish year-to-year consistency. Baty finished 2025 on the IL due to an oblique issue, but that shouldn't affect his availability for the start of 2026.

name: Kyle Manzardo
season_outlook: Manzardo exhausted his rookie eligibility with 156 plate appearances in 2024, but he got in his first full MLB campaign last season and produced 27 home runs, 70 RBI, 47 runs and a .234/.313/.455 slash line in 142 games. He did most of his damage against right-handed pitching with a .789 OPS, though he still slugged .419 versus lefties. Manzardo doesn't offer much defensively but still made 56 appearances at first base, so he'll have eligibility there rather than solely as a designated hitter. He should be a steady presence in Cleveland's lineup in 2026 but may not have true everyday volume given his struggles against southpaws, though his power potential could help him see more chances than a standard platoon player.

name: Zach McKinstry
season_outlook: McKinstry is a sneaky late-round pick in deeper mixed leagues, particularly those that use roto scoring, thanks to his positional flexibility -- he qualifies at three different spots -- and stolen base contributions. He has swiped at least 16 bases in each of the last three seasons and had 46 extra-base hits in 2025, while registering personal bests in most offensive categories. McKinstry’s contact quality remains only mediocre, however, and his statistical profile lacks much in the way of matchups he can exploit. Regard him as a back-of-your-roster type, but not a player likely to make many advances in 2026.

name: Jordan Lawlar
season_outlook: Numerous factors have worked against Lawlar getting an extended chance in Arizona, from Eugenio Suarez’s handling third base in 2024, to Lawlar’s thumb surgery last spring, to his own need to find another defensive position. A onetime top-10 overall prospect, Lawlar will experiment in the outfield in the hopes the Diamondbacks can jump start his career. He hit .313/.403/.564 with 11 homers and 20 steals in 63 games for Triple-A Reno last season, and he’s still only 23 years old, so don’t forget about him as a prospective breakthrough candidate if he’s looking good during Cactus League play.

name: Colt Emerson
season_outlook: Emerson is the type of prospect who is very good at many things yet lacks eye-popping skills or stats in any one department. He hit .285/.383/.458 with 16 homers and 14 steals in 130 games across three minor-league levels in the Mariners system in 2025, all while playing solid shortstop. With a strong spring showing, Emerson could either break camp with the team or earn himself an early-season promotion, though his 20 years of age say he might need some time to get fully acclimated to MLB pitching. Nevertheless, he's a top dynasty prospect and a surefire add in all redraft leagues once he does arrive.

name: Spencer Horwitz
season_outlook: February surgery derailed Horwitz’s chances at being a fantasy sleeper last spring and, upon his return in mid-May, he put up near-identical numbers to those from his encouraging 2024. While he has a great plate approach -- a handy skill for points-based fantasy play -- his contact-quality metrics are average at best. That’s a problem for a player who calls an extreme pitchers’ park his home. Horwitz, no longer a second baseman after just one appearance there in 2025, is a corner infielder for deeper mixed leagues.

name: Jesus Sanchez
season_outlook: Sanchez was in the midst of a typical season for the Marlins in 2025 with 10 homers, nine steals and a .256/.320/.420 slash line through 86 games, but he was traded to the Astros at the summer deadline and never got on track with his new team, batting .199 and finishing with a .611 OPS in 48 games for Houston. Sanchez's production prior to the trade was pretty close to the .750 OPS he posted the two previous seasons, so it's reasonable to expect him to rebound to that level in 2026, especially given the small sample with the Astros. He isn't likely to see much action versus left-handed pitching but should see enough volume to be fantasy relevant as a strong-side platoon player, assuming he beats out Nathan Lukes for the left field job in Toronto. Sanchez doesn't have a ton of upside but is a decent target to round out a fantasy outfield.

name: Logan O'Hoppe
season_outlook: O'Hoppe hit 19 home runs while operating as the Angels' primary catcher in 2025, but he batted just .213 and provided horrible run production with 43 RBI and 35 runs. His strikeout and walk rates (30.8 percent and 5.4 percent, respectively) also left a lot to be desired, and the underwhelming production resulted in veteran Travis d'Arnaud taking on a larger role than initially expected. O'Hoppe's batted-ball data was still strong however, so there's reason to believe he can get back on track in 2026. That being said, he would seem to have a limited ceiling since his power is modest, and he isn't likely to stand out in batting average or run production.

name: Andrew Benintendi
season_outlook: Benintendi's time on the South Side has been forgettable, as he's been essentially a replacement-level player in all three years with the club. The left fielder began 2025 with an Opening Day homer but hit the injured list less than two weeks into the season with an adductor strain. He made a second trip to the IL in May with a calf strain, and a third at the end campaign with Achilles tendinitis. Benintendi managed to reach 20 homers for the second consecutive season despite all the missed time, but he hit .240 as his move to add flyballs in recent years has been a severe detriment to his batting average. Even the White Sox don't play him every single day, often shielding him from lefties. Benintendi will remain part of the regular lineup versus right-handed pitching as the club runs out the clock on his remaining two years under contract.

name: Lars Nootbaar
season_outlook: Nootbaar played in a career-high 135 games in 2025, but his fantasy production dropped despite the increased volume since his .686 OPS was nearly 90 points worse than his career mark entering the season. Even though he had 80 more plate appearances than any other season, he saw his counting stats remain the about same, finishing with 13 home runs, 48 RBI and 68 runs while slugging just .361. However, Nootbaar still ranked near the top of the league in hard-hit rate (50 percent) and average exit velocity (91.3 mph), which puts him in a strong position to rebound in 2026. He underwent surgery on both heels in October and isn't guaranteed to be fully recovered by Opening Day, so his rehab progress is worth monitoring.

name: Cedric Mullins
season_outlook: After years of Camden Yards inflating his power numbers -- he has hit 64 of his 103 career homers there -- Mullins' mediocre metrics in that department were exposed following his midseason trade to the Mets. He hit just .182/.284/.281 in 42 games for the Mets, and those park translations carry some worry now that he'll play for the Tropicana Field-housed Rays. Mullins remains a good enough defender with 30-steal speed to remain a solid roto late-rounder, but his points-league value has taken a hit in his new digs.

name: Harrison Bader
season_outlook: Bader stayed healthy for long enough last season to play in a career-high 146 games, showcasing elite defense while stealing double-digit bases for the fourth consecutive year. He also put forth the best underlying power metrics he has in nine seasons in the majors. Bader’s rising strikeout rate, however, makes him increasingly a batting average risk, and the move to San Francisco lands him in one of the game’s worst power environments. Fantasy managers should value Bader closer to his three-year average than 2025 alone, as he’ll contribute in the primary roto categories, but without much in the way of upside.

name: Tyler Stephenson
season_outlook: Stephenson bounced back in 2024 with 19 homers and a .782 OPS in 138 games, but he got off to a rocky start last season as an oblique injury delayed his debut until May. He then missed time during the second half due to a fractured thumb, and he wasn't quite as productive when available with a .231/.316/.421 slash line in 88 contests. Stephenson still provided quality power and run production with 13 home runs, 50 RBI and 40 runs, but a 33.9 percent strikeout rate was a career worst by a significant margin. Stephenson should be able to get back to 2024 levels if he can stay healthy, though he likely won't be relied upon as a true everyday catcher given his injury history. He has every incentive to put it all together in 2026, which is his final year of arbitration eligibility.

name: Ryan McMahon
season_outlook: After years of trade rumors, the Rockies finally dealt McMahon at the summer deadline in 2025, sending him to the Yankees. His production remained largely the same in 2025, though his .214 average was a career worst, while he did club 20 home runs for a sixth straight full season. Despite the decent power numbers, he continues to showcase limited upside for run production with 53 RBI and 62 runs. However, landing in the Bronx certainly raises that ceiling even with him likely to hit toward the bottom of the lineup. McMahon's defense at third base brings the Yankees defensive stability, so he should receive plenty of opportunities again in 2026. Fantasy managers just shouldn't expect him to move the needle significantly.

name: Carlos Narvaez
season_outlook: Narvaez was acquired from the Yankees in a rare trade between longtime AL East rivals and opened the season as Connor Wong's backup, but Wong's early injury and subsequent struggles allowed Narvaez to seize the regular catching job. He delivered a modest 97 wRC+ yet still batted cleanup for a month during a strong second-half run. His barrel and hard-hit rates sit slightly above average, though his aggressive chase tendencies create too much swing-and-miss and cap his offensive output. Narvaez is slated to be the primary catcher this season, and while Wong held that role a year ago before regressing, Narvaez offers a stronger skill set and is the superior defender, even finishing as a Gold Glove finalist. He profiles as a cost-effective No. 2 catcher in mixed leagues.

name: Colton Cowser
season_outlook: A year after playing 153 games, Cowser was limited to just 92 due to a fractured thumb, a rib issue and a concussion. He broke his thumb sliding into first base on Opening Day weekend and missed just over two months. He collided with an outfield wall in early August and missed over a week due to a concussion. Earlier in the season, he also ran into an outfield wall and hurt his ribs without an IL stint. After the season, it was revealed he fractured two ribs, which may explain his .197/.273/.384 line for the rest of the season, though his production was even worse in the prior nine games, five of which came after returning from his thumb injury. A rising strikeout rate drove last season's decline. With 14 steals in 14 attempts, Cowser offers five-category upside, but the strikeouts create a shaky floor.

name: Connor Norby
season_outlook: Norby's trial run in Miami after being acquired at the 2024 trade deadline went well with a .760 OPS, but his first full season with the club in 2025 was less productive with a .251/.300/.389 slash line. He was limited to 88 games due to oblique, wrist and quad injuries, and he clubbed just eight home runs while recording eight stolen bases, 34 RBI and 42 runs. He improved his strikeout rate to 26.7 percent, and it's possible the injuries played a role in his power drop. Norby should be able to provide double-digit homers and steals if he can stay on the field in 2026, but any production beyond that isn't guaranteed and may not come with strong ratios.

name: Victor Scott II
season_outlook: Scott got off to a hot start in 2025 with a .290/.357/.403 slash line, two homers, 11 steals, 18 RBI and 20 runs in his first 37 games, but he struggled to a .529 OPS in 101 contests the rest of the season. He still provided single-category fantasy value with a total of 34 stolen bases, but his .296 slugging percentage was the worst in baseball among players with at least 450 plate appearances. Scott's strong defense in center field should help him to retain a regular role in the outfield for the rebuilding Cardinals, but the organization could look to see what else it has if he doesn't make some improvements at the plate.

name: Walker Jenkins
season_outlook: Jenkins, the Twins' first-round pick in 2023 and one of baseball's top-rated prospects each year since, has dealt with his share of injuries thus far as a pro, but his .295/.399/.464 line through 192 career minor-league games underscore his massive offensive potential when healthy. Assuming better luck in the injury department, he should be ready to break into the rebuilding Twins outfield before midseason. Jenkins' skill set should play well in points leagues, and he's a potential five-category player for roto formats as well. Be sure to add him the moment he's promoted.

name: Matt Wallner
season_outlook: Wallner received his longest look in the majors in 2025 and clubbed 22 home runs in 104 games, but his numbers were otherwise pretty underwhelming with a .202 average, 40 RBI and 47 runs. His 29.1 percent strikeout rate was actually a major improvement from 2024, and he also had a strong 12 percent walk rate. The swing-and-miss in his stroke is obvious, but Wallner consistently makes strong contact when he connects and has a good eye at the plate. He actually fared better versus left-handed pitching than right (.790 OPS vs. .771 OPS), so he may be able to avoid a platoon. Wallner may not end up providing fantasy managers with much production outside of home runs, but the upside is there for him to do more, and the opportunities should be there on the rebuilding Twins.

name: Keibert Ruiz
season_outlook: Ruiz's skills are closer to those of a reserve infielder. Few players, regardless of position, put the ball in play more, but he does so with very little authority. In prior seasons he leaned flyball, which supported modest power, but last year he hit grounders just under half the time, and as one of the slowest runners in the league he didn't beat many out. In late June, Ruiz was hit in the head by a line drive while in the dugout and missed the rest of the season on the concussion IL, though he's expected to be cleared by camp. A long-term contract should keep him in the mix, but the Nationals acquired Harry Ford to compete with Ruiz for time behind the plate.

name: Sean Murphy
season_outlook: Murphy hasn't quite been the elite catcher Atlanta was expecting when it traded for him and signed him to a six-year extension in December of 2022, as he delivered a second straight season of underwhelming numbers in 2025. The veteran backstop played in just 94 games and missed the final weeks of the season to undergo surgery for a right hip labral tear, but the emergence of Drake Baldwin played a bigger role in his reduced playing time throughout the season. Murphy launched 16 home runs, but he batted below .200 for a second straight year and had a career-worst 31.2 percent strikeout rate. It's possible the hip surgery he underwent could help him to get back on track since he had been playing through the injury for years, but he appears likely to miss at least the first month of the season. At this point a best-case scenario likely would be Murphy serving in a timeshare at catcher with Baldwin once healthy, with their respective 2025 performances pointing toward Baldwin as the lead horse.

name: Josh Lowe
season_outlook: Lowe showcased his potential during his first full MLB season in 2023 with 20 homers, 32 steals and an .835 OPS, but the past two years have been marred by injury and poor production. The outfielder had two more IL stints in 2025 due to oblique issues and was limited to 108 games. He struggled at the plate when available, posting a .220/.283/.366 slash line, though he still provided fantasy managers with a bit of power and speed with 11 home runs and 18 stolen bases. Lowe's main upside at this point is steals as he has 79 in 403 career games. He is simply unplayable against lefties (.459 OPS in 2025), so his volume is going to be capped by a platoon even if he can stay healthy. Lowe can provide fantasy managers some value if everything is going right, but the past two seasons have showcased how low his floor can be, and he may not have much longer of a leash with the Rays.

name: Masataka Yoshida
season_outlook: A shoulder injury cost Yoshida half of 2025, though he’d finish on a high note, batting .354/.369/.494 in his final 23 regular-season and Wild Card Series games. While he figures to be Boston’s DH against right-handed pitching, keep their cluttered first base and outfield pictures in mind, as further missed time or any struggles could result in a dip in playing time. Yoshida is best used as a matchups option in daily formats, but he’s worth taking in the late rounds of deep mixed leagues.

name: Anthony Santander
season_outlook: Santander was one of the biggest signings of last winter as he landed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Blue Jays, but his first campaign in Toronto was a disaster with a .175/.271/.294 slash line and just six homers, and his second will see him on the injured list for most of the year following February left labral surgery. Once he heals, Santander will have every opportunity to get back on track for Toronto given what remains of his contract, and the surrounding lineup should offer plenty of opportunities for counting stats.

name: Triston Casas
season_outlook: A ruptured patella tendon ended Casas’ 2025 in early May, ending what was a disappointing season only shortly after it began, and threatens to cut into the opening weeks and possibly months of 2026. The Red Sox, reacting to this, acquired Willson Contreras to handle first base, meaning Casas will have to fight for at-bats between first base and DH if he’s to recapture what had previously been massive power upside. Entering the year, Casas is one of the riskiest picks around and he’s better left to deep mixed or AL-only drafts until we get more definitive word on his health.

name: Nick Castellanos
season_outlook: Philadelphia did everything possible to show that Castellanos was not in the plans for 2026, and released him just before spring training. The Padres picked him up shortly afterward, with the idea that he'd compete for platoon at-bats between right field, first base and DH. Castellanos' new home should allow him to at least hit homers and drive in runs, but the skills decline here is real, so tread carefully.

name: Lenyn Sosa
season_outlook: Granted a starting role for the first time over the final three-plus months of last season -- he started 74 of the White Sox’s final 82 games between 1B, 2B and DH -- Sosa exploded for 18 home runs and 58 RBI. That RBI total was the most among 2B-eligible players over that time. Unfortunately, it came with some of the worst plate discipline in baseball, and an HR/FB rate more than 2% greater than the league average, making him a top regression candidate. Sosa’s skill set can be handy for filling out a roto lineup, but he’d need more patience to be a similar contributor in points leagues.

name: Sebastian Walcott
season_outlook: The Rangers could have themselves a future left-side-of-the-infield gem in Walcott, though his ascent to Arlington appears likely to wait until 2027 after February UCL surgery on his right elbow. For dynasty purposes, Walcott is a potential five-category roto standout who hit .255/.355/.386 with 10 homers and 32 steals in 124 games for Double-A Frisco last season. And before you say "well, that's hardly an eye-popping hitting line," bear in mind that he was once again one of the very youngest players at his competitive level. Walcott's injury and young age could cause a slow adjustment to the majors once he arrives, but his upside is so great, he's still a top-shelf dynasty stash.

name: Aidan Miller
season_outlook: Miller's skill set should be especially appealing in roto play, as he's a speedy prospect who swiped 59 bases in 116 games between Double-A Reading and Triple-A Lehigh Valley last season. Scouts see him developing more power upside from the 14 homers and .433 slugging percentage he had there. He's a shortstop for now, but might figure into the Phillies' third base plans at some point during the year, making him a worthy dynasty pick.

name: Gavin Lux
season_outlook: Lux's first year with the Reds didn't look all that different from his time with the Dodgers after he was traded in January. He played in a career-high 140 games and had a .269/.350/.374 slash line, with his five home runs being half the total he posted in 2024. He also tallied 53 RBI and 49 runs scored while doing most of his damage against right-handed pitching (.761 OPS vs. RHP and .466 OPS vs. LHP). Lux's 11.2 percent walk rate gives him some lineup stability, but the lack of counting stats limits his fantasy upside. He split most of his playing time between left field and designated hitter, with just 17 appearances at second base removing his eligibility there in most leagues. Lux is a high-floor, low-ceiling player that is likely to be limited to a strong-side platoon unless he can reverse his career-long struggles versus southpaws.

name: Tyler O'Neill
season_outlook: O'Neill landed with the Orioles last winter on a three-year, $49.5 million contract, but the first season of that deal was a complete disaster. The veteran outfielder played in just 54 games due to shoulder and wrist injuries, which were just the latest in an extensive injury history. O'Neill was unproductive when available, delivering nine home runs with four steals, 26 RBI, 22 runs and a .684 OPS in 209 plate appearances. The underlying numbers indicate O'Neill had some unfortunate luck with a .218 BABIP, but that's only part of the equation here. He's played 100 games in a season just twice since making his MLB debut in 2018, as he's simply been unable to stay healthy for any considerable length of time. The Orioles don't seem like they'll be counting on the outfielder to fill an everyday role in 2026 following the offseason acquisitions of Taylor Ward and Pete Alonso, and a more niche role like that could help O'Neill to stay healthy, albeit with an obvious hit to his volume.

name: Parker Meadows
season_outlook: Meadows was limited to 58 games in 2025 due to arm and quadriceps injuries, but it wasn't much better when he was healthy with a .215/.291/.300 slash line. He posted just four home runs and four steals in 213 plate appearances, with a 26.3 percent strikeout rate being the worst of his three MLB campaigns. Meadows illustrated his power and speed potential in 2024 with nine home runs and nine stolen bases over 82 games, but he's yet to show that he can consistently perform at that level in the majors. His reliable defense in center field should help him to maintain playing time, but the Tigers may not wait too long to test their other options if his offensive struggles carry over into 2026. Beyond that, there's also the question of whether or not Meadows can stay healthy.

name: Sung-Mun Song
season_outlook: Back-to-back big years in Korea, at the ages of 27 and 28, put Song firmly on the MLB radar, and the Padres saw his defensive utility as a boon to their offense. He managed a 25/25 season overseas in 2025, and he has a good chance at breaking camp as the Padres’ second baseman, if not a rotating starter all over their infield. Monitor Song’s progress in adapting to MLB pitching during spring training, as he’d be a late-round sleeper if he looks ready to play every day.
